messages.subject: reshape()-type function for matrices?
messages.subject_clean: reshape()-type function for matrices?
messages.body_plain:
Hi list. Is there any way to turn a matrix that's say, 4 x 8 into one that's 16 x 2?

In R I'd do:

A = matrix(1:32,4,8) # initialize A
matrix(A, 16,2) # reshape it

And in matlab:

A = reshape([1:32],4,8); % initialize A
reshape(A,16,2) % reshape it

I know about to_vector in Stan, which I could use to turn a matrix that's 4 x 8 into a vector of length 32. I guess to_matrix will turn that into a 32 x 1 matrix. But I don't see a to_matrix that'll reshape it...

Thanks,
Seth

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] reshape()-type function for matrices?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] reshape()-type function for matrices?
messages.body_plain:
We definitely don't plan to reshape existing matrices.
Once a matrix is declared, its size can't change.

May I ask what you need it for?

We could write something that would build a matrix
from an array and maybe go back and forth that way,
as in:

  matrix[4,8] A;
  matrix[16,2] B;
  B <- as_matrix(16,2, to_vector(A));

That would respect the current type system, but
wouldn't be as efficient as just writing loops (at least
until we get deep support of matrix expression templates).

I find this kind of thing confusing because of the
column- vs. row-major orientations.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] reshape()-type function for matrices?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] reshape()-type function for matrices?
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to implement Kronecker-vector products using matrix-vector algebra. Explanation is here: http://www.mathcs.emory.edu/~nagy/courses/fall10/515/KroneckerIntro.pdf and more here: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vectorization_(mathematics)

So I guess your proposal would work. Given:

    matrix[3,3] X;
    matrix[2,2] Y;
    vector[6] v;

Let \otimes denote Kronecker product. Then to calculate (X \otimes Y)v I'd do:

    to_vector(X * as_matrix(4, 3, to_vector(transpose(Y * as_matrix(3, 4, v))))

But is there some reason to not allow as_matrix(...) to take a matrix directly:

as_matrix(p,q, X) := as_matrix(p,q, to_vector(X))?

I agree column- vs row-major orientation is hard to keep track of, but I think in all of these cases it's column-major, because that's what the vec operator does--it stacks columns of a matrix into a vector.

(Note that it's actually possible at present to do (X \otimes Y)v in Stan by defining v as matrix[3,4] and then using to_vector at the end, but I don't think it's possible to do (X \otimes Y \otimes Z) v because that requires a reshape step.)

Seth

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the pointers.

It makes sense to me to have to_matrix accept a matrix argument
with an implicit to_vector.

What we don't need is another overload of the term "vectorization"!

It would also make sense to encapsulate all of this inside
a C++ function that's specialized.

Matrices and ordering are column major in Stan (inherited
from the default for  Eigen::Matrix).  Arrays, on the other hand,
are row major, inherited std::vector.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Jan 2, 2015, at 10:59 PM, Cody Ross <ctr...@ucdavis.edu> wrote:
>
> This is probably a pretty basic question to someone with experience, but I am struggling with interpreting some parameters. Normally, I would ignore the parameter values and examine predictions, but this time I really need to focus on the parameters themselves.
>
> The model:
> ############################### Loop over years
>  for (y in 1:Y){
> ############################### Learning Equation
>  for(m in 1:(M-1)){
>    Alpha[m] <- Theta[p,m,1] +  Theta[p,m,2]*Ifr_local[m,(y-1)] + Theta[p,m,3]*Iwr2_local[m,(y-1)] + Theta[p,m,4]*Sfr[m,(y-1)] + Theta[p,m,5]*Swr[m,(y-1)] + Theta[p,m,6]*Pfr[m,(y-1)] + Theta[p,m,7]*Pwr[m,(y-1)];
>               }
>    Alpha[M] <- 0;
>
>    I2_local ~ multinomial(softmax(Alpha));
>       }
>
> Alpha, is this case, is a vector to be turned into a simplex, and is used to pass information to the probability statement at each pass through the loop.
>
> The Thetas are unique to a category (m), and a person (p). Right now I'm using K-1 vectors, by fixing the last category to zero, prior to running the softmax.
>
> Each kind of data in the model is on the unit interval, so it would be nice if I could compare the importance of each kind of data to the outcome simply by comparing the absolute value of the parameters, both across categories and across data types within a category; however, I'm not sure if this is possible if I fix one category to zero by fiat. So the questions are:
>
> 1. What is the interpretation of the Theta parameters as I have written them... What are the units?

It helps to look at a binary case and then extend intuitions.
In the binary case, the Alpha are log odds, as in the linear
predictor for a logistic regression.  This highlights that the Theta are
just logistic regression coefficients, which is something like change in
log odds per unit of predictor they're being multiplied by.  So if the
predictor is height, then it's change in log odds per unit height.

Going beyond binary, the Alpha are still log odds vs. the final outcome, but
this doesn't give you an overall marginal probability, just log odds
vs. the distinguished outcome.  But, the theta are still interpretable in
the same units.  They're still change in log odds per unit of predictor, only
now it's log odds vs. the distinguished outcome.

> 2. If I were to use regularizing priors and K vectors instead, what would be the interpretation of the Theta parameters then?

The Alpha don't have the same clean interpretation any more, as
they're only interpretable relative to each other.  Without the prior,
they're only identified up to adding a constant to each.  The theta
are still regression coefficients, though, and still have the same units,
namely change in log odds per unit of predictor.

- Bob

hessian() in stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp treats all model values as if they
are free. For example, if you have a 2 dimensional multivariate normal
density then there are 5 potential parameters, 2 means and the lower
triangle of the covariance matrix (2 variance and 1 covariance).
However, suppose one of the variances is fixed to 1. Ideally, the
Hessian should omit any pairs involving the fixed variance.

Is there any C++ API facility to omit fixed parameters? Is something
planned?

--

messages.body_plain:
For me, it's more about modularity.  The model isn't part
of the R code --- the R code's a script to run the model.
I often run the same model over different data sets and
like to have a script per data set calling the same external
model.

I personally don't like embedding R scripts directly in knitr/sweave
docs for the same reason.

For those of us who want to debug using CmdStan (more direct),
we have to cut and paste out of the R string.  And usually try
to figure out how to recreate a standalone data set.

I like the emacs mode for Stan, but that's only relevant
if you use emacs (we've had requests to do it as an embedded
mode in ESS).

There's no fundamental reason not to use it --- using a file
essentially just reads the model string out of the file and
passes it to our C++ translator.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] autodiff, optimization
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] autodiff, optimization
messages.body_plain:
There is no easy way to optimize this and it's not clear that it's worth it.  Either Sigma is a parameter (in which case, it needs to be refactorized each time) or it's data (in which case the factorization is likely not a major cost unless the dimensionality is huge).

Also, note that right now hessian() uses a finite diff approximation to the Hessian.  In the (hopefully near) future it will use autodiff and avoid this issue altogether.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Hierarchical Model: Convergence Problem
messages.subject_clean: Hierarchical Model: Convergence Problem
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I wonder whether you can help me to find a solution for the convergence problem of the attached hierarchical model using a simple simulated data set. The data aims to simulate allele counts of rare and common genetic variants and its effects on blood pressure.

Using the IWLS-EM algorithm of the R/BhGLM package [1], the model converges easily with correct results with less than 4 iterations and less than 1 second run-time (results not shown). However, the NUTS algorithm of the R/STAN (V2.4.0) package strongly overestimates the parameters with two chains and 10,000 iterations running for 20 hours. I have attached the R/STAN script and output (for 1000 iterations, about 2 hours).

My understanding is, that just adding more iterations won't solve the problem, but the HMC/NUTS algorithm has to be configured/tuned for this problem. I was actually expecting much better performance of the HMC/NUTS sampler for hierarchical models with highly correlated parameters.

Any help is much appreciated!

Best regards and a happy New Year!

Will

References:
[1] http://www.ssg.uab.edu/bhglm/files/BhGLM_1.1.0.zip

messages.body_plain:
You're right --- more iterations won't help.

There will be a convergence problem due to the
multiplicative non-identifiability of gamma and alpha.
if you multiply gamma[1] by C and divide alpha[1] by C,
you get the same linear predictor.

The Cauchy priors aren't strong enough to pin down the
values.

As you can see in your output, the posterior 95%
intervals are very wide for the parameters.

This is usually bad news.  There's a chapter in the
manual on problematic posteriors.

I don't see what the gamma are giving you here as only
the product of gamma and alpha is identified in the likelihood.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Dear Bob,

thanks for your advice! The idea of this model is to separate effects of individual genetic variants and grouped genetic variants, especially to increase the power of detecting effects of rare variants with sparse data, similar to testing a genetic risk score  (see Paper PMID 22144906). Your arguments why this model is not well-identified sound convincing, however, I wonder why this model can be easily fitted with the R/BHGLM (IWLS-EM algorithm) package which uses a very similar setup (although the prior variances are constructed as hierarchical (half)Cauchy distributions, which shared hyperparameters per group), so my impression was that it has to do something with the algorithm.

Apart from convergence problems with STAN, my simulations (with the R/BGHLM package) show that when using weakly informative priors (Cauchy(0,1)), the fraction of Bayesian p values with p < 0.05 is considerably higher, which  in my opinion indicates an overfitting problem because the group effect and the variant effects are estimated from the same data.

Do you also see a problem there?

Best, Will

messages.body_plain:

If you are using a multinormal prior, then it is best to post-multiply independent standard normals by the Cholesky factor and shift by the mean vector.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Relative efficiencies of multi_normal_cholesky, multi_normal_prec and multi_normal
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Relative efficiencies of multi_normal_cholesky, multi_normal_prec and multi_normal
messages.body_plain:
Actually, even multi_normal_prec needs to perform a matrix factorization if Sigma is a parameter to compute the log(det(Sigma)) term.

In general it is best to use the version that is most natural.  If you have an inverse covariance matrix, use multi_normal_prec, if you have (or need) the cholesky factor for other reasons, use multi_normal_cholesky.  If you end up calling multi_normal many times with the same covariance matrix, it is *sometimes* worth computing the Cholesky factorization of Sigma once and using multi_normal_cholesky but not often.

Finally, if you start fiddling to make your models "fast" be sure to actually time things.  Because of the complexity of how Stan works, some seeming optimizations can actually make things much slower.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Mon, Jan 5, 2015 at 9:30 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> multi_normal_prec() tends to be faster because you don't have to invert a matrix / solve a system of equations. But that is only for the likelihood. If you are using a multinormal prior, then it is best to post-multiply independent standard normals by the Cholesky factor and shift by the mean vector.
>
> Ben
>
>

> > The manual says that multi_normal_cholesky is more efficient than multi_normal but what is the relative efficiency of multi_normal_prec to both of these?
> >
> > Thanks,
> > John.

messages.body_plain:
Also, if you can vectorize, it'll help with all three parameterizations.
That way, Stan only has to do the factorization once for all of the outcomes.

So rather than

for (n in 1:N)
  y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu[n], Sigma);

it's much faster to use:

  y ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);

with more advantage as N grows.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] autodiff, optimization
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] autodiff, optimization
messages.body_plain:
You're looking at two different things.

Joshua is talking about the hessian() function in autodiff.hpp,
and it is indeed as he describes it.

Marcus is talking about our use of the Hessian to calculate
Laplace approximations to covariance at a mode.

To answer Joshua's original question, each time the density is evaluated,
it's with a different forward-mode variable configuration.  As far as we
can tell, it's not possible to reuse a factorization with our current
reverse-nested-in-forward autodiff setup for Hessians.

We're working on a new approach to autodiff which is much faster
for Hessians (an order of magnitude or more) for just this reason.

- Bob

> On Jan 5, 2015, at 5:53 AM, Joshua N Pritikin <jpri...@pobox.com> wrote:

>> issue altogether.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Hierarchical Model: Convergence Problem
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Hierarchical Model: Convergence Problem
messages.body_plain:
> On Jan 5, 2015, at 4:13 AM, Wilmar Igl <wilma...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Bob,
>
> thanks for your advice! The idea of this model is to separate effects of individual genetic variants and grouped genetic variants, especially to increase the power of detecting effects of rare variants with sparse data, similar to testing a genetic risk score  (see Paper PMID 22144906). Your arguments why this model is not well-identified sound convincing, however, I wonder why this model can be easily fitted with the R/BHGLM (IWLS-EM algorithm) package which uses a very similar setup (although the prior variances are constructed as hierarchical (half)Cauchy distributions, which shared hyperparameters per group), so my impression was that it has to do something with the algorithm.

I don't know BHGLM, and its home page only provides a zip, no indication
of what the algorithm is.  But IWLS-EM sounds like an optimization algorithm,
not an MCMC sampler.   Because there are priors, there's a well-defined
maximum likelihood set of parameters.  And optimization is much much faster
than MCMC in general.

You can try Stan's optimizer and see what happens.  Usually you can't
optimize a hierarchical model, so maybe BHGLM is doing something more
like marginal maximum likelihood, since it claims to be handling hierarchical
models.  There you usually maximize one set of params while marginalizing
out the other, then use the data again to fit the other set of parameters
conditioned on the max of the first:

  target:   p(alpha,beta|data)

  alpha* = ARGMAX_alpha INTEGRAL p(alpha,beta|data) d.beta

  beta* = ARGMAX p(beta|alpha,data)

But a posterior mode isn't the same as a Bayesian posterior mean.
And an MML solution is a different thing again.

> Apart from convergence problems with STAN, my simulations (with the R/BGHLM package) show that when using weakly informative priors (Cauchy(0,1)), the fraction of Bayesian p values with p < 0.05 is considerably higher,

Higher than what?

> which  in my opinion indicates an overfitting problem because the group effect and the variant effects are estimated from the same data.
>
> Do you also see a problem there?

Stan doesn't use the data twice.

In full Bayesian inference (as opposed to, say maximum
penalized likelihood or maximum marginal likelihood), you only
use the data once to fit the entire model.

- Bob

models and to compare them, but we can't provide
a tutorial via e-mail.  There are lots of resources
out there on Bayes.  See, e.g., Gelman et al.'s
Bayesian Data Analysis book or the BUGS book.  We
particularly like cross-validation-based measures, of
which WAIC is an approximation.  And informal measures
like posterior predictive checking.

Yes, you can compute things like chi-squared tests and
also look at posterior intervals if you want.

A 200GB Hessian would entail something north of 150K params?
We should probably work on saving half the space in the Hessian
storage.

There's nothing built-in to do Hessians on only some params
that I know of.

The best you could do is compute it yourself by taking
finite differences based on the gradients.  That's pretty
much what's going on under the hood at the moment anyway
in RStan.

We will be replacing the finite-diffs approach with one
based on 2nd order autodiff that should be more efficient.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Diagnosing slow performance
messages.body_plain:
The manual explains the stages that warmup goes through.  There's
a part near the end with a chapter on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and
how it's implemented in Stan.

The only thing you can control is how long the various stages
are and where you start in terms of step size.   But this might
be enough to control your issues for a particular model.

What's happening early on is that you're probably needing to
find a very small step size before the scales are adapted per
parameter.  This means multiple leapfrog steps per iteration.
Then, once Stan's sorted out the scales, it can increase the
step size and thus cut down on the number of leapfrog steps.

Another thing that can help is scaling the data so all the parameters
are roughly on the unit scale.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

It looks to me that you use a too short warmup phase of only 100 steps. As far as I recall, Stan shuts off quite important warmup adjustments if you warmup less than 250 iterations. Could you check what the elements of the mass matrix are? I remember that with less than 250 warmup iterations then I only got a diagonal mass matrix. Only with more than 250 warmup iterations Stan will make a smart guess on the mass matrix which is really important for good performance during sampling.

You can make Stan use less than 250 warmup iterations to come up with an adjusted mass matrix if you play around with the different windows (phases) during warmup - Michael is the expert here. However, I never dared to play with this and simply always go with at least 250 warmups. This situation will become better once we can pass into Stan a mass matrix manually, but that is on the todo list as far as  I recall.

Best,
Sebastian

> On Jan 7, 2015, at 11:02 AM, He-chien Tsai <depo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks for reply. I think WAIC is similiar to AIC and BIC.

> They just tell me which one is the best in a collection of models and don't show anything about whether all models in that collection are bad.

Not quite.  WAIC provides an approximation of cross-validation
performance.  And it does it with the proper posterior instead of
point estimates.

You can use that to compare if you want.

> I'm looking for a method for whether I should accept or reject a model like p-value or significance level. I guess something like that must exists in bayesian approach but I don't know the name.

You can use things like chi-square tests if you insist on trying
to reject a model.

Nothing's going to tell you to accept a model, frequentist or Bayesian.

Models are typically approximations that can always be rejected with
enough data.

- Bob

messages.subject: Another WAIC question (time series?)
messages.subject_clean: Another WAIC question (time series?)
messages.body_plain:
After reading the Gelman, Hwang, and Vehtari paper on predictive information criteria (which is great by the way), I'm trying to think about the appropriateness of WAIC in the following (pretty common) context:

Suppose we have J groups and T time periods, so y[t,j] is the observed value of y at time t for group j. (We also have predictors x[t,j].) I'm wondering if WAIC is appropriate in this scenario assuming that our interest in predictive accuracy is for existing groups only (i.e. we might get data for new time periods but only for the same J groups). My hunch is that this scenario requires a more complicated form of cross-validation that WAIC does not approximate, but the more I think about it the more confused I seem to become. Am I right that WAIC is not appropriate here?

Thanks in advance for any advice!

messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to fit a fairly simple multilevel logistic regression model (attached) to data from a perception experiment using PyStan. The model consists of listener, stimulus-category, stimulus-talker, and various parent parameters. I tried to include the following transformed parameters block to calculate the predicted probability (this block is in the attached file, commented out). The arrays sb, st, and tk contain indices for the listener, stimulus category, and stimulus talker, respectively.

transformed parameters {
    row_vector<lower=0,upper=1>[ntr] theta[nsb]; // predicted probability
    for(sbi in 1:nsb)
        for(tri in 1:ntr)
            theta[sbi,tri] = inv_logit(beta[sb[sbi]] + alpha[st[sbi,tri],tk[sbi,tri]]);
}

However, I got the following error. I tried it with theta defined as real<lower=0,upper=1> theta[nsb,ntr] and got the same error. I also tried it with curly brackets enclosing the nested loops, but that didn't help.

> > ValueError: Error parsing model code:
> > SYNTAX ERROR, MESSAGE(S) FROM PARSER:
> > Illegal statement beginning with non-void expression parsed as
> >   get_base1(get_base1(theta,sbi,"theta",1),tri,"theta",2)
> > Not a legal assignment, sampling, or function statement.  Note that
> >   * Assignment statements only allow variables (with optional indexes) on the left;
> >     if you see an outer function logical_lt (<) with negated (-) second argument,
> >     it indicates an assignment statement A <- B with illegal left
> >     side A parsed as expression (A < (-B)).
> >   * Sampling statements allow arbitrary value-denoting expressions on the left.
> >   * Functions used as statements must be declared to have void returns
> >
> >
> > ERROR at line 23
> >  21:        for(sbi in 1:nsb)
> >  22:            for(tri in 1:ntr)
> >  23:                theta[sbi,tri] = inv_logit(beta[sb[sbi]] + alpha[st[sbi,tri],tk[sbi,tri]]);
> >                     ^
> >  24:    }

The attached model works, with the inv_logit() term used as an argument to the bernoulli() distribution function (i.e., it compiles and I can get samples of the posterior distribution). I was able to get a similar model working using a transformed parameters block much like this using RStan a while back. Any ideas about why this is causing problems here would be appreciated, as would thoughts and suggestions about the pros and cons of constructing this kind of model with or without the transformed parameters block.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Diagnosing slow performance
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Diagnosing slow performance
messages.body_plain:
Sebastian,

Some of my experiments did use a warmup phase of only 100 steps, and I'm disregarding the results of those runs for the reasons you mention. The more recent experiments I've run have all used 1000 warmup plus 1000 sampling iterations.

A lesson here for anyone else diagnosing slow performance: Running for 100+100 iterations doesn't tell you anything useful about what will happen when you run for 1000+1000 iterations.

On Wednesday, January 7, 2015 3:04:44 AM UTC-7, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Hi!
>
> It looks to me that you use a too short warmup phase of only 100 steps. As far as I recall, Stan shuts off quite important warmup adjustments if you warmup less than 250 iterations. Could you check what the elements of the mass matrix are? I remember that with less than 250 warmup iterations then I only got a diagonal mass matrix. Only with more than 250 warmup iterations Stan will make a smart guess on the mass matrix which is really important for good performance during sampling.
>
> You can make Stan use less than 250 warmup iterations to come up with an adjusted mass matrix if you play around with the different windows (phases) during warmup - Michael is the expert here. However, I never dared to play with this and simply always go with at least 250 warmups. This situation will become better once we can pass into Stan a mass matrix manually, but that is on the todo list as far as  I recall.
>
> Best,
> Sebastian
>
> On Wednesday, January 7, 2015 1:08:30 AM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > The manual explains the stages that warmup goes through.  There's
> > a part near the end with a chapter on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and
> > how it's implemented in Stan.
> >
> > The only thing you can control is how long the various stages
> > are and where you start in terms of step size.   But this might
> > be enough to control your issues for a particular model.
> >
> > What's happening early on is that you're probably needing to
> > find a very small step size before the scales are adapted per
> > parameter.  This means multiple leapfrog steps per iteration.
> > Then, once Stan's sorted out the scales, it can increase the
> > step size and thus cut down on the number of leapfrog steps.
> >
> > Another thing that can help is scaling the data so all the parameters
> > are roughly on the unit scale.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > > On Jan 6, 2015, at 5:30 PM, Kevin Van Horn <ke...@ksvanhorn.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > I have some more information on this. With a simplified version of the model running for 1000+1000 iterations I found:
> > >
> > > * Average n_leapfrog__, first 100 warmup iterations: 1310.
> > >
> > > * Average n_leapfrog__, remaining 1900 iterations: 65.
> > >
> > > The sum of n_leapfrog__ over the first 100 iterations is greater than the sum over all remaining iterations. Looking at a plot of n_leapfrog__, I see a sudden drop after iteration 100 in each of the four chains.
> > >
> > > Any ideas why the first 100 iterations would average 20 times as many leapfrog steps as later iterations? Or what I could do to improve that?
> > >
> > > More context: the simplification was that I restricted the covariance matrix for the regression coefficients to be diagonal. I ran 4 chains and made an effort to get reasonably good initial values.
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, December 23, 2014 1:58:46 PM UTC-7, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> > > The mixing looks pretty good. I have weakly informative priors, and I've already reparameterized. Nearly two hours ago I started another test run with max_treedepth set to 13, and three of the chains are at somewhere between iteration 40 and 60, with the other one somewhere between iteration 20 and 40; that works out to at least 170 seconds per iteration for the slowest chain. (I'm running the chains in parallel.)
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, December 23, 2014 12:25:30 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > There are two issues:  speed of the implementation code and
> > > speed of the model.
> > >
> > > The 1000+ leapfrog steps are the problem because Stan's
> > > evaluating log probs and gradients for each of those steps.
> > > The only way to fix this is to reparameterize or tighten priors.
> > >
> > > More warmup iterations might help.  Starting at a lower step
> > > size might also help the warmup go faster.
> > >
> > > How is the mixing?  I'd suggest making the treedepth bound even
> > > higher.  I hope it maxing out at different numbers in warmup and
> > > during sampling isn't indicative of an off-by-one error in config
> > > (won't affect sampling accuracy---just how deep the tree can grow
> > > in NUTS).
> > >
> > > - Bob

> > > > On Dec 23, 2014, at 1:29 PM, Kevin Van Horn <ke...@ksvanhorn.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > I am running a nested multinomial logit model with a hierarchical prior and I am getting very slow performance. Mixing looks good, but it's averaging around 80 seconds for ONE iteration. This is a problem with 8 choice tasks for each of 1620 individuals, with each task being a choice between 3 alternatives and "none", and each alternative described by a total of 23 covariates (after appropriately encoding discrete attributes). I have tried all of the optimization tricks mentioned in the Stan user manual that appear relevant.

Thank you for the tips! I implemented Carpenter's code suggestions (attached) and got roughly a 20% speed improvement per iteration and no apparent change in convergence speed for the parameter sigma_series (which is very very low). After about an hour, effective sample size is still in the single digits. Are there any other possible speedups?

On Tuesday, January 6, 2015 12:51:30 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The problem in your model is that you have this:
>
> >     real<lower=0> sigma_series;
> ...
> >    sigma_series~uniform(0,.01);
>
>
> The declared constraints on a variable (here (0,inf)) should match
> its support in the model (here (0,0.01)).  You need to declare
> sigma_series as
>
>   real<lower=0,upper=0.01> sigma_series;
>
> at which point the uniform(0,0.01) is redundant (though doesn't
> hurt much as Stan can figure out at compile time that everything
> other than size checks on sigma_series are redundant.
>
> Are you sure the right answer is in that range and not butting
> up against a boundary?  We'd usually recommend an unconstrained
> sigma_series and a softer constraint, say
>
>   sigma_series ~ cauchy(0,0.005);
>
> Same issue with sigma.
>
> I'm not sure why you're dividing by sqrt of sample size
> for the std devs in the model, but if you need to do it,
> I'd recommend computing an inverse sqrt size vector in transformed
> data and then multiplying that by sigma.  You should probably move
> the transformed parameters to local variables in the model --- I
> don't see any reason to save them, which is what declaring them
> as transformed parameters does.
>
> > for(i in 1:num_series)
> >       z[i,1]~normal(0,.05);
> > for(i in 1:num_series)
> >   for(t in 2:num_periods)
>       z[i,t]~normal(z[i,t-1],sigma_series);
>
> This can be sped up considerably by rewriting as:
>
>   col(z,i) ~ normal(0, 0.05);
>   for (i in 1:num_series)
>     head(z[i],num_periods-1) ~ normal(tail(z[i],num_periods-1), sigma_series);
>
> It's most efficient here if z is declared as an
> array of vectors, because then there's no copying or
> non-local memory required to compute z[i].
>
> - Bob
>
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Diagnosing slow performance
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Diagnosing slow performance
messages.body_plain:
Bob,

This was very useful information. To verify that different scales for the different parameters was the issue, I tried optimally scaling the (untransformed) parameters. Specifically, for each parameter I found the posterior mean and std dev from a previous run and did a new run with parameters scaled to all have a posterior s.d. of 1. This made a substantial difference:

* The initial run had a total of 523,977 leapfrog steps summed over the first 100 iterations of all four chains; 492,946 leapfrog steps summed over the remaining 900+1000 iterations of all four chains; and a total of 1,016,923 leapfrog steps summed over all iterations and all chains.

* The run with optimal scaling had a total of 27,212 leapfrog steps summed over the first 100 iterations of all four chains; 484,120 leapfrog steps summed over the remaining 900+1000 iterations of all four chains; and a total of 511,332 leapfrog steps summed over all iterations and all chains.

So optimal scaling reduced the total computational effort to about half.

Of course, you don't know the optimal scaling in advance, but this suggests to me that it really can be worthwhile to get some idea of the width of the posterior for each parameter and scale accordingly.

As a guide for anyone else who might want to experiment with this kind of thing, here are some details:

The original model had the following parameters block:

    parameters {
      matrix[K+1, R] Epsilon;
      real<lower=0, upper=1> lambda;
      vector<lower=0>[K+1] sigma;
      matrix[K+1, G] preTheta;
    }

I did an initial run of 1000 warmup and 1000 sampling iterations, with the result stored in the variable "fit", then executed this code to find the posterior widths:

    samples <- extract(fit)
    mu.Epsilon <- apply(samples$Epsilon, 2:3, mean)
    sd.Epsilon <- apply(samples$Epsilon, 2:3, sd)
    mu.logit.lambda <- mean(logit(samples$lambda))
    sd.logit.lambda <- sd(logit(samples$lambda))
    mu.log.sigma <- colMeans(log(samples$sigma))
    sd.log.sigma <- apply(log(samples$sigma), 2, sd)
    mu.preTheta <- apply(samples$preTheta, 2:3, mean)
    sd.preTheta <- apply(samples$preTheta, 2:3, sd)

For the optimal scaling run, I made modifications to the data, parameters, and transformed parameters sections of the model. I added the following to the data block:

    data {
      ...
      matrix[K+1, R] mu_Epsilon;
      matrix<lower=0>[K+1, R] sd_Epsilon;
      real mu_logit_lambda;
      real<lower=0> sd_logit_lambda;
      vector[K+1] mu_log_sigma;
      vector<lower=0>[K+1] sd_log_sigma;
      matrix[K+1,G] mu_preTheta;
      matrix<lower=0>[K+1,G] sd_preTheta;
    }

I changed the parameters block to be

    parameters {
      matrix[K+1, R] scaled_Epsilon;
      real scaled_logit_lambda;
      vector[K+1] scaled_log_sigma;
      matrix[K+1, G] scaled_preTheta;
    }

and added these lines to the "transformed parameters" block:

    transformed parameters {
      matrix[K+1, R] Epsilon;
      matrix[K+1, G] preTheta;
      vector[K+1] log_sigma;
      vector<lower=0>[K+1] sigma;
      real<lower=0, upper=1> lambda;
      ...

      Epsilon <- mu_Epsilon + sd_Epsilon .* scaled_Epsilon;
      preTheta <- mu_preTheta + sd_preTheta .* scaled_preTheta;
      log_sigma <- mu_log_sigma + sd_log_sigma .* scaled_log_sigma;
      sigma <- exp(log_sigma);
      lambda <- inv_logit(mu_logit_lambda + sd_logit_lambda * scaled_logit_lambda);

      ...
    }

Finally, since the model block includes prior distributions for sigma and lambda, which are now transformed parameters, I included a Jacobian adjustment:

    model {
      lambda ~ uniform(0, 1);
      increment_log_prob(log(lambda * (1 - lambda)));
      sigma ~ normal(0, 5);
      increment_log_prob(log_sigma);
      ...

    }

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Another WAIC question (time series?)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Another WAIC question (time series?)
messages.body_plain:
What I've seen done in natural language problems evaluations
is to predict/model outcome at time n given all of the
the observations from time 1 to n-1.  Then you can plot the
posterior predictive log probability

  log p(y[n] | y[1],...,y[n-1])

at times t[1], ..., t[N].

Rather than giving you a proper cross-validation, it gives you
something like a learning curve for the predictions.

Another thing you can do is fit all of the rest of the data

  log p(y[n], y[n+1], ..., y[N] | y[1],...,y[n-1])

though if you plot you probably want to divide by (N - n + 1) to
scale everything to average prediction.  It gives you a posterior
predictive cross-entropy rate estimate of the data vs. the model.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to determine goodness of fit?
messages.body_plain:
> I don't get this. If that's true, what's p-value actually for?

They’re for confusing poor statistics students.

> It also sounds like that every experiment's result by p-value are not confident because every model can always be rejected with enough data.

Yup.  That’s why most practical Bayesians don’t take their models too seriously.

> Despite that, I'd like to know what are the most common methods for bayesians to try rejecting a model. Although I found a paper titled "A BAYESIAN χ2 TEST FOR GOODNESS-OF-FIT", I seldom heard this test is used.

Proper Bayesians DO NOT reject models.  Like any hypothesis/significance test,
p-values require that you define both a null hypothesis and a competing hypothesis.
With the competing hypothesis you can compute the power of any testing procedure
which calibrates the resulting p-value.  In a Bayesian setting the null hypothesis is
the full model and there is no competing hypothesis (which would have to be something
like “every other possible model excluding the null” which may not even be expressible
mathematically).  This lack of calibration also effects cross-validation, WAIC, and the
like which is why they can only ever be used for comparisons.

Again, proper Bayesians do not reject models.  Instead we criticize models, looking
for tension with prior beliefs or predictive performance to expand and grow our model.

Hi Bob,

Regarding your first suggestion (predicting the outcome at time t conditional on the observations before t), I'm wondering what the best way is to implement something like this (using R and Stan). My first thought is to loop over the time periods in R and, for each one, run the model in Stan using the data up to that time, predicting the next outcome in generated quantities. So a very simplified version of this might be something like this:

Stan code :

# Note: I just wrote this out to be as simple as possible, so not worried about priors, optimizing code, or even if the model itself makes much sense, etc.

data {
  int<lower=1> T ; // time periods
  int<lower=1> J ; // groups
  matrix[T,J] y ; // outcome
  matrix[T,J] x ; // predictor
  vector[J] x_next ; // predictor at next time period T+1
}
parameters {
  real a ;
  real b ;
  real c ;
  real<lower=0> sigma ;
}
model {
  for (j in 1:J) // loop over groups
   for (t in 2:T) // loop over time
    y[t,j] ~ normal(a + b * y[t-1, j] + c * x[t, j], sigma) ;
}

generated quantities {
  vector[J] y_next_pred ;
  for (j in 1:J)
    y_next_pred[j] <- normal_rng(a + b * y[T, j] + c * x_next[j], sigma) ;
}

R pseudo-ish code:

T <- number of time periods

stan_save <- list()

stan_compile <- compile C++ code

for (t in 2:(T-1)) { # start at 2 because we need obs n-1 in the likelihood

  data_t <- list(y = y[1:t, ],  x = x[1:t, ],  x_next = x[t+1, ], J = J, T = t)

  stan_out <- stan(fit = stan_compile, data = data_t, pars = c(“y_next_pred”), whatever other arguments ... )

  stan_save[[t-1]] <- extract(stan_out)

}

Am I on the right track here?

Thanks again for the help!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to determine goodness of fit?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How to determine goodness of fit?
messages.body_plain:
Snarkiness aside, here is what actually happened to me when I presented posterior credible intervals for the parameter of interest (using Stan) in my papers and alongside the interval, I presented p=Prob(b>0) (the posterior probability of the parameter being greater than zero given data), I got the comment, but this is a one-sided significance test; please present the two-tailed test: 1-2*min( P(b<0), P(b>0).

Since that didn't make any sense at all, I just added the results of the likelihood ratio test based chi-squared using lmer. I think that's a reasonable compromise, because it gives the researcher used to p-values something to look at that they are familiar with at least for making their decision, and at the same time it just presents the amount of information available from the data as a credible interval. Maybe over time the shift will happen, but for now maybe that's good enough. The bottom line seems to be that if I don't want to just stick my results into the proverbial drawer (i.e., "publish papers"), I am going to have to report p-values *alongside* the posterior credible intervals.

If anyone has any better ideas on what to say/do to respond to the criticism that P(b>0) is a one-sided significance test---other than pointing out the obvious fact that it is not---I'm listening.

messages.subject_clean: New psycholinguistics paper using Stan
messages.body_plain:
@article{FrankEtAl2015,
  author = {Stefan L. Frank and Thijs Trompenaars and Shravan Vasishth},
  title = {Cross-linguistic differences in processing double-embedded relative clauses: {W}orking-memory constraints or language statistics?},
  year = {2015},
  pages = {n/a},
  abstract = {An English double-embedded relative clause from which the middle verb is omitted can often be processed more easily than its grammatical counterpart, a phenomenon known as the grammaticality illusion. This effect has been found to be reversed in German, suggesting that the illusion is language specific rather than a consequence of universal working memory constraints. We present results from three self-paced reading experiments which show that Dutch native speakers also do not show the grammaticality illusion in Dutch, whereas both German and Dutch native speakers do show the illusion when reading English sentences. These findings provide evidence against working memory constraints as an explanation for the observed effect in English. We propose an alternative account based on the statisti- cal patterns of the languages involved. In support of this alternative, a single recurrent neural network model that is trained on both Dutch and English sentences indeed predicts the cross-linguistic difference in grammaticality effect.},
  journal = {Cognitive Science},
  note = {accepted pending minor revisions},
 code = {https://github.com/vasishth/StanJAGSexamples/tree/master/FrankEtAlCogSci2015},
  pdf = {http://www.ling.uni-potsdam.de/~vasishth/pdfs/FrankTrompenaarsVasishthCogSci.pdf}
}

I will make data and other R code available as soon as the paper is in press.

messages.subject: Exponentially Modified Normal Distribution
messages.subject_clean: Exponentially Modified Normal Distribution
messages.body_plain:
This may be a silly question, but is there any reason why the Exponentially Modified Normal pdf is:

f(x | \mu, \sigma, \tau) = \frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{\pi}} exp\Big(\frac{\lambda}{2}(2\mu + \lambda\sigma^2 -2x)\Big) erfc\Big(\frac{\mu + \lambda\sigma^2 -x}{\sqrt{2}\sigma} \Big)

whereas on Wikipedia <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponentially_modified_Gaussian_distribution>, the pdf is:

f(x | \mu, \sigma, \tau) = \frac{\lambda}{2} exp\Big(\frac{\lambda}{2}(2\mu + \lambda\sigma^2 -2x)\Big) erfc\Big(\frac{\mu + \lambda\sigma^2 -x}{\sqrt{2}\sigma} \Big)

i.e. Stan lambda is divided by sqrt(pi), in the Wikipedia formula by 2.

Has anybody already implemented a multivariate Poisson distribution in Stan? It would perhaps be useful for other types of models as well.

- Max

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] n-mixture model in Stan? [marginalizing
messages.body_plain:
Nope, we don't have a multivariate Poisson (all the functions
we do have are organized by type in the manual).

What is a multivariate Poisson?  If it's like a multi-logistic-normal,
it's easy to express in Stan:

  vector[N] mu;
  cov_matrix[N] Sigma;
  vector[N] y;
  vector[N] lambda;

  lambda ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);
  y ~ poisson_log(lambda);

And of course you could replace mu with x * beta where x is a data matrix and
beta a coefficient vector if you wanted to do a linear model of the means, say.

- Bob

> On Jan 9, 2015, at 10:23 AM, Maxwell Joseph <maxwell...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks to the authors of the following paper, it seems that N-mixture models an also be fit with a multivariate Poisson distribution that requires no infinite sums, and no discrete parameters:
>
> Dennis EB, Morgan BJT, Ridout MS (2014) Computational aspects of N-mixture models. Biometrics (early view): http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/biom.12246/full
>
> Has anybody already implemented a multivariate Poisson distribution in Stan? It would perhaps be useful for other types of models as well.
>
> - Max
>
> On Monday, January 13, 2014 at 9:36:03 AM UTC-7, Chris Roy wrote:
> The N-mixture model is quite popular in ecology for point counts (bird surveys), aerial surveys, camera traps, etc. From my experience I would say that N tend to be low generally ranging from 0 to 20's for point counts and camera traps. Numbers might be higher for large airscale surveys but I'm pretty sure that numbers in the 100's are quite rare.
>
> I also agree that ecology can be quite messy. That means that pure N-mitxture model are rather rare and ecologists often have to deal with zero-dispersion and zero-inflation when trying to fit those models.
>
> Chris
> -------------
>
>
>
> On Mon, Jan 13, 2014 at 6:02 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>
> On 1/12/14, 11:01 PM, David J. Harris wrote:
> One data point: I'm pretty sure my undergrad stats textbook said it was okay to use a Gaussian whenever lambda exceeded
> 5 (admittedly this book, was far too fond of Gaussian approximations).  There may also be a continuity correction that
> can make it even closer.
>
> That's usually qualified by making sure p isn't near a boundary for
> obvious reasons of the (0,1) constraints.  Of course, with enough data,
> even then it should be OK.   Other authors suggest more than 5.
> So I think these approximations should be OK.  The Wikipedia has the
> usual discussion:
>
> Poisson:  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution#Related_distributions
>
> Binomial:  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_distribution#Normal_approximation
>
>
>
> I don't know if Kéry and Royle would agree with me, but my feeling is this: ecology is often quite messy.  If lambda is
> mostly in the tens or hundreds, and this is the most egregious approximation they're making, they're in fabulous shape.
> Finding a closed-form version would be nice, but it probably wouldn't change the inferences too much.
>
> That was my thinking, but I'm a computer scientist, not an
> experienced applied statistician.
>
>
> If they're dealing with a species whose local abundance tends to be lower than that, then it could be worth the effort

> We can do the brute-force marginalization for small N.
>
>
> - Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Another WAIC question (time series?)
messages.body_plain:
> On Jan 8, 2015, at 4:44 PM, Jonah <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob,
>
> Regarding your first suggestion (predicting the outcome at time t conditional on the observations before t), I'm wondering what the best way is to implement something like this (using R and Stan). My first thought is to loop over the time periods in R and, for each one, run the model in Stan using the data up to that time, predicting the next outcome in generated quantities.

In outline, that's the only way I can think to make it work.
But I didn't understand the details of what you were doing below.

I'd have thought you'd set up a model like this:

  int T;
  real t[T];  // times t
  int T_last;
  real x[T];  // predictors
  real y[T];  // outcomes

  model {
    head(y,T_last) ~ normal(mu,sigma);

  generated quantities {
    double ll;
    ll <- normal_log(tail(y,T-T_last), mu, sigma);

This is a really simple model that doesn't actually have a time
series model per se, but it illustrates the general point of using
the first 1...T_last items to estimate parameters (here mu and sigma)
and then use those parameters to estimate the log density of the
rest of the data from times T_last + 1 ... T.

- Bob

> So a very simplified version of this might be something like this:
>
> Stan code :
>
>
> # Note: I just wrote this out to be as simple as possible, so not worried about priors, optimizing code, or even if the model itself makes much sense, etc.
>
> data {
>   int<lower=1> T ; // time periods
>   int<lower=1> J ; // groups
>   matrix[T,J] y ; // outcome
>   matrix[T,J] x ; // predictor
>   vector[J] x_next ; // predictor at next time period T+1
> }
> parameters {
>   real a ;
>   real b ;
>   real c ;
>   real<lower=0> sigma ;
> }
> model {
>   for (j in 1:J) // loop over groups
>    for (t in 2:T) // loop over time
>     y[t,j] ~ normal(a + b * y[t-1, j] + c * x[t, j], sigma) ;
> }
>
> generated quantities {
>   vector[J] y_next_pred ;
>   for (j in 1:J)
>     y_next_pred[j] <- normal_rng(a + b * y[T, j] + c * x_next[j], sigma) ;
> }

I'd have coded this differently for this purpose, with:

>
>
> R pseudo-ish code:

> stan_save <- list()
>
>
> stan_compile <- compile C++ code
>
>
> T <- number of time periods
>
> for (t in 2:(T-1)) { # start at 2 because we need obs n-1 in the likelihood
>
>
>   data_t <- list(y = y[1:t, ],  x = x[1:t, ],  x_next = x[t+1, ], J = J, T = t)
>
>   stan_out <- stan(fit = stan_compile, data = data_t, pars = c(“y_next_pred”), whatever other arguments ... )
>
>   stan_save[[t-1]] <- extract(stan_out)
>
>
> }
>
>
>
>
> Am I on the right track here?
>
> Thanks again for the help!
>
>

> On Thursday, January 8, 2015 at 12:47:31 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What I've seen done in natural language problems evaluations
> is to predict/model outcome at time n given all of the
> the observations from time 1 to n-1.  Then you can plot the
> posterior predictive log probability
>
>   log p(y[n] | y[1],...,y[n-1])
>
> at times t[1], ..., t[N].
>
> Rather than giving you a proper cross-validation, it gives you
> something like a learning curve for the predictions.
>
> Another thing you can do is fit all of the rest of the data
>
>   log p(y[n], y[n+1], ..., y[N] | y[1],...,y[n-1])
>
> though if you plot you probably want to divide by (N - n + 1) to
> scale everything to average prediction.  It gives you a posterior
> predictive cross-entropy rate estimate of the data vs. the model.
>
> - Bob
>
>

Y = Y_0 + Y_2

then (X, Y) ~ BivariatePoisson(\theta_0, \theta_1, \theta_2), and

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Diagnosing slow performance
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Diagnosing slow performance
messages.body_plain:
Let me just summarize a few of the key points here.

Warmup:

Conceptually MCMC warmup times are basically equivalent to
the autocorrelation time — because HMC chains tend to be
lowly autocorrelated they also tend to converge really, really
quickly.

The HUGE caveat is that such an argument assumes uniformity
of curvature across the parameter space, as assumption which
is violated in many of the complex models we see.  Very often
the tails have large curvature while the bulk is relatively
well-behaved; in other words, warmup is slow not because
the actual convergence time is slow but rather because the
cost of an HMC iteration is more expensive out in the tails.

Poor behavior in the tails is the kind of pathology that Andrew
notes we can find by running only a few warmup iterations.
By looking at the acceptance probabilities and step sizes of
the first few iterations you can get an idea of how bad the
problem is and whether you need to address it with modeling
efforts.

The Mass Matrix (or, more formally, the Euclidean Metric):

The mass matrix can compensate for linear (i.e. global)
correlations in the posterior which can dramatically improve
the performance of HMC in some problems.  Of course this
requires that we know the global correlations a priori.

In complex models this is incredibly difficult (for example,
nonlinear model components convolve the scales of the
data, so standardizing the data doesn’t always help) so in
Stan we learn these correlations online with an adaptive
warmup.  In models with strong nonlinear (i.e. local)
correlations this learning can be slow, even with regularization.
This is ultimately why warmup in Stan often needs to be
so long, and why a sufficiently long warmup can yield such
substantial performance improvements.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] n-mixture model in Stan? [marginalizing
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] n-mixture model in Stan? [marginalizing
messages.body_plain:
Here's a start - recovers the true parameters well, but could probably be more efficiently constructed. This specification lacks covariates, so there are only three parameters: theta_1, theta_2, and theta_3. This is a general case of a bivariate Poisson, rather than the specific parameterization for N-mixture model equivalence given by Dennis et al. 2014. The bivariate Poisson corresponds to an N-mixture model with two repeated surveys. With R repeated surveys, you'd need an R-dimensional multivariate Poisson. I'm going to see if I can implement that case with covariates, but this might be useful for people interested in the bivariate Poisson, but not interested in N-mixture models. Here's a gist <https://gist.github.com/mbjoseph/100a41d73901764a00a7> of the same script. The parameterization below corresponds to the likelihood:

 <https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-qnpkiis2f64/VLIBFLDNNMI/AAAAAAAAAwQ/wR4QsQURTJs/s1600/likelihood.png>

## Simple bivariate poisson model in stan
## following parameterization in Karlis and Ntzoufras 2003
## Simulate data
n <- 50

# indpendent poisson components
theta <- c(2, 3, 1)

X_i <- array(dim=c(n, 3))
for (i in 1:3){
  X_i[,i] <- rpois(n, theta[i])
}

# summation to produce bivariate poisson RVs
Y_1 <- X_i[, 1] + X_i[, 3]
Y_2 <- X_i[, 2] + X_i[, 3]

Y <- matrix(c(Y_1, Y_2),
            ncol=n,
            byrow=T)

# Trick to generate a ragged array-esque set of indices for interior sum
# we want to use a matrix operation to calculate the inner sum
# (from 0 to min(y_1[i], y_2[i])) for each of i observations
minima <- apply(Y, 2, min)
u <- NULL
which_n <- NULL
for (i in 1:n){
  indices <- 0:minima[i]
  u <- c(u, indices)
  which_n <- c(which_n,
               rep(i, length(indices))
               )
}

length_u <- length(u) # should be sum(minima) + n

# construct matrix of indicators to ensure proper summation
u_mat <- array(dim=c(n, length_u))
for (i in 1:n){
  u_mat[i, ] <- ifelse(which_n == i, 1, 0)
}

# plot data
library(epade)
bar3d.ade(Y_1, Y_2, wall=3)

 <https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-TcGxs0UqmUk/VLH8kSFt6HI/AAAAAAAAAvs/jDZ0KCsfALQ/s1600/data_dist.png>

# write model statement
cat(
  "
data {
  int<lower=1> n;                 // number of observations
  vector<lower=0>[n] Y[2];        // observations
  int length_u;                   // number of u indices to get inner summand
  vector<lower=0>[length_u] u;    // u indices
  int<lower=0> which_n[length_u]; // corresponding site indices
  matrix[n, length_u] u_mat;      // matrix of indicators to facilitate summation
}

parameters {
  vector<lower=0>[3] theta;       // expected values for component responses
}

transformed parameters {
  real theta_sum;
  vector[3] log_theta;
  vector[n] u_sum;
  vector[length_u] u_terms;

  theta_sum <- sum(theta);
  log_theta <- log(theta);

  for (i in 1:length_u){
    u_terms[i] <- exp(binomial_coefficient_log(Y[1, which_n[i]], u[i]) +
                      binomial_coefficient_log(Y[2, which_n[i]], u[i]) +
                      lgamma(u[i] + 1) +
                      u[i] * (log_theta[3] - log_theta[1] - log_theta[2]));
  }
  u_sum <- u_mat * u_terms;
}

model {
  vector[n] loglik_el;
  real loglik;
  for (i in 1:n){
    loglik_el[i] <- Y[1, i] * log_theta[1] - lgamma(Y[1, i] + 1) +
                  Y[2, i] * log_theta[2] - lgamma(Y[2, i] + 1) +
                  log(u_sum[i]);
  }
  loglik <- sum(loglik_el) - n*theta_sum;
  increment_log_prob(loglik);
}
  ", file="mvpois.stan")

# estimate parameters
library(rstan)
d <- list(Y=Y, n=n, length_u=length_u, u=u, u_mat=u_mat, which_n=which_n)
init <- stan("mvpois.stan", data = d, chains=0)
mod <- stan(fit=init,
            data=d,
            iter=2000, chains=3,
            pars=c("theta"))
traceplot(mod, "theta", inc_warmup=F)

# evaluate parameter recovery
post <- extract(mod)
par(mfrow=c(1, 3))
for (i in 1:3){
  plot(density(post$theta[, i]))
  abline(v=theta[i], col="red")
}
par(mfrow=c(1, 1))

library(scales)
pairs(rbind(post$theta, theta),
      cex=c(rep(1, nrow(post$theta)), 2),
      pch=c(rep(1, nrow(post$theta)), 19),
      col=c(rep(alpha("black", .2), nrow(post$theta)), "red"),
      labels=c(expression(theta[1]), expression(theta[2]), expression(theta[3]))
      )

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-92eYoUBcI-A/VLH9Cuky2nI/AAAAAAAAAv8/eWRxizAPSMQ/s1600/recov.png>

> > The multivariate Poisson is not quite the same as a multi-logistic normal. It was described formally by Kawamura in 1979 (http://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.kmj/1138036064).
> >
> > Here's a slide show that gives a quick overview: http://www.stat-athens.aueb.gr/~karlis/multivariate%20Poisson%20models.pdf
> >
> > Below is the probability function for a bivariate Poisson:
> >
> > If
> >
> > X_i ~ Poisson(\theta_i) for i =0, 1, 2
> >
> > and we define X and Y as
> >
> > X = X_0 + X_1
> > Y = Y_0 + Y_2
> >
> > then (X, Y) ~ BivariatePoisson(\theta_0, \theta_1, \theta_2), and
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Friday, January 9, 2015 at 2:12:49 PM UTC-7, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > Interesting, perhaps a good example for the manual/book.
> >
> >> On Jan 9, 2015, at 10:23 AM, Maxwell Joseph <maxwell...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> Thanks to the authors of the following paper, it seems that N-mixture models an also be fit with a multivariate Poisson distribution that requires no infinite sums, and no discrete parameters:
> >>
> >> Dennis EB, Morgan BJT, Ridout MS (2014) Computational aspects of N-mixture models. Biometrics (early view): http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/biom.12246/full
> >>
> >> Has anybody already implemented a multivariate Poisson distribution in Stan? It would perhaps be useful for other types of models as well.
> >>
> >> - Max
> >>
> >> On Monday, January 13, 2014 at 9:36:03 AM UTC-7, Chris Roy wrote:
> >> The N-mixture model is quite popular in ecology for point counts (bird surveys), aerial surveys, camera traps, etc. From my experience I would say that N tend to be low generally ranging from 0 to 20's for point counts and camera traps. Numbers might be higher for large airscale surveys but I'm pretty sure that numbers in the 100's are quite rare.
> >>
> >> I also agree that ecology can be quite messy. That means that pure N-mitxture model are rather rare and ecologists often have to deal with zero-dispersion and zero-inflation when trying to fit those models.
> >>
> >> Chris
> >> -------------
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> On Mon, Jan 13, 2014 at 6:02 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >>
> >>
> >> On 1/12/14, 11:01 PM, David J. Harris wrote:
> >> One data point: I'm pretty sure my undergrad stats textbook said it was okay to use a Gaussian whenever lambda exceeded
> >> 5 (admittedly this book, was far too fond of Gaussian approximations).  There may also be a continuity correction that
> >> can make it even closer.
> >>
> >> That's usually qualified by making sure p isn't near a boundary for
> >> obvious reasons of the (0,1) constraints.  Of course, with enough data,
> >> even then it should be OK.   Other authors suggest more than 5.
> >> So I think these approximations should be OK.  The Wikipedia has the
> >> usual discussion:
> >>
> >> Poisson:  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution#Related_distributions
> >>
> >> Binomial:  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_distribution#Normal_approximation
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> I don't know if Kéry and Royle would agree with me, but my feeling is this: ecology is often quite messy.  If lambda is
> >> mostly in the tens or hundreds, and this is the most egregious approximation they're making, they're in fabulous shape.
> >> Finding a closed-form version would be nice, but it probably wouldn't change the inferences too much.
> >>
> >> That was my thinking, but I'm a computer scientist, not an
> >> experienced applied statistician.
> >>
> >>
> >> If they're dealing with a species whose local abundance tends to be lower than that, then it could be worth the effort
> >> to find a closed-form alternative.
> >>
> >> We can do the brute-force marginalization for small N.
> >>
> >>

messages.body_plain:
[changed subject so people can find it in the future]

Thanks for the nice example and writeup.

I have one piece of advice:  always work on the log scale
when you can.  Things like binomial coefficients and gamma are prone
to overflow when taken off the log scale, so exp() is always a red flag.
Here's the program excerpt:

> data {
...

>  matrix[n, length_u] u_mat;      // matrix of indicators to facilitate summation
> }
> parameters {
>  vector<lower=0>[3] theta;       // expected values for component responses
> }
> transformed parameters {

...
>  vector[length_u] u_terms;

>

>  for (i in 1:length_u){
>    u_terms[i] <- exp(binomial_coefficient_log(Y[1, which_n[i]], u[i]) +
>                      binomial_coefficient_log(Y[2, which_n[i]], u[i]) +
>                      lgamma(u[i] + 1) +
>                      u[i] * (log_theta[3] - log_theta[1] - log_theta[2]));
>  }
>  u_sum <- u_mat * u_terms;
> }
>
>
> model {

...
>                  log(u_sum[i]);
>  }

Formatting wise, the "+" signs can go on the next line following standard
math notation --- unlike R, Stan can handle run-on expressions like this because
we have the ";" for a line-termination marker.

The robust way to write this is with the log_sum_exp operation.  So
just leave u_terms on the log scale, defining a variable:

> for (i in 1:length_u)

>   log_u_terms[i] <- binomial_coefficient_log(Y[1, which_n[i]], u[i])

>                     + binomial_coefficient_log(Y[2, which_n[i]], u[i])
>                     + lgamma(u[i] + 1) +
>                     + u[i] * (log_theta[3] - log_theta[1] - log_theta[2]));

And then noting that

 u_sum[i] = u_mat[i] * u_terms,

so that

 log(u_sum[i]) = log(u_mat[i] * u_terms)

and noting that u_mat[i] is a row vector and u_terms a vector, you get

 log(u_sum[i]) = log(SUM_k u_mat[i,k] * u_terms[k])

               = log(SUM_k exp(log(u_mat[i,k] * u_terms[k])))

               = log(SUM_k exp(log(u_mat[i,k]) + log(u_terms[k])))

               = log_sum_exp(log(u_mat[i]) + log_u_terms)

which should all execute without overflow anywhere.  You'll want to recompute
u_mat on the log scale as transformed data and create an array of vectors,
as in:

 transformed data {
   vector[length_u] log_u_mat[N];
   for (n in ...)
     for (m in ...)
       log_u_mat[n,m] <- log(u_mat[n,m]);

to do this most efficiently (there's a chapter on arrays vs. matrices
and efficiency in the manual).

You'll want to recompute u_mat on the log scale rather than literally
taking the log of it each time.

You should get the same answer, though!

- Bob

> On Jan 11, 2015, at 12:05 AM, Maxwell Joseph <maxwell...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Here's a start - recovers the true parameters well, but could probably be more efficiently constructed. This specification lacks covariates, so there are only three parameters: theta_1, theta_2, and theta_3. This is a general case of a bivariate Poisson, rather than the specific parameterization for N-mixture model equivalence given by Dennis et al. 2014. The bivariate Poisson corresponds to an N-mixture model with two repeated surveys. With R repeated surveys, you'd need an R-dimensional multivariate Poisson. I'm going to see if I can implement that case with covariates, but this might be useful for people interested in the bivariate Poisson, but not interested in N-mixture models. Here's a gist of the same script. The parameterization below corresponds to the likelihood:
>
>
>
>
>
>

> ## Simple bivariate poisson model in stan
> ## following parameterization in Karlis and Ntzoufras 2003
> ## Simulate data
> n <- 50
>
>
> # indpendent poisson components
> theta <- c(2, 3, 1)
>
>
> X_i <- array(dim=c(n, 3))
> for (i in 1:3){
>  X_i[,i] <- rpois(n, theta[i])
> }
>
>
> # summation to produce bivariate poisson RVs
> Y_1 <- X_i[, 1] + X_i[, 3]
> Y_2 <- X_i[, 2] + X_i[, 3]
>
>
> Y <- matrix(c(Y_1, Y_2),
>            ncol=n,
>            byrow=T)
>
>
> # Trick to generate a ragged array-esque set of indices for interior sum
> # we want to use a matrix operation to calculate the inner sum
> # (from 0 to min(y_1[i], y_2[i])) for each of i observations
> minima <- apply(Y, 2, min)
> u <- NULL
> which_n <- NULL
> for (i in 1:n){
>  indices <- 0:minima[i]
>  u <- c(u, indices)
>  which_n <- c(which_n,
>               rep(i, length(indices))
>               )
> }
>
>
> length_u <- length(u) # should be sum(minima) + n
>
>
> # construct matrix of indicators to ensure proper summation
> u_mat <- array(dim=c(n, length_u))
> for (i in 1:n){
>  u_mat[i, ] <- ifelse(which_n == i, 1, 0)
> }
>
>
> # plot data
> library(epade)
> bar3d.ade(Y_1, Y_2, wall=3)
>
>
>
>

> # write model statement
> cat(
>  "
> data {
>  int<lower=1> n;                 // number of observations
>  vector<lower=0>[n] Y[2];        // observations
>  int length_u;                   // number of u indices to get inner summand
>  vector<lower=0>[length_u] u;    // u indices
>  int<lower=0> which_n[length_u]; // corresponding site indices
>  matrix[n, length_u] u_mat;      // matrix of indicators to facilitate summation
> }
>
>
> parameters {
>  vector<lower=0>[3] theta;       // expected values for component responses
> }
>
>
> transformed parameters {
>  real theta_sum;
>  vector[3] log_theta;
>  vector[n] u_sum;
>  vector[length_u] u_terms;
>
>
>  theta_sum <- sum(theta);
>  log_theta <- log(theta);
>
>
>  for (i in 1:length_u){
>    u_terms[i] <- exp(binomial_coefficient_log(Y[1, which_n[i]], u[i]) +
>                      binomial_coefficient_log(Y[2, which_n[i]], u[i]) +
>                      lgamma(u[i] + 1) +
>                      u[i] * (log_theta[3] - log_theta[1] - log_theta[2]));
>  }
>  u_sum <- u_mat * u_terms;
> }
>
>
> model {
>  vector[n] loglik_el;
>  real loglik;
>  for (i in 1:n){
>    loglik_el[i] <- Y[1, i] * log_theta[1] - lgamma(Y[1, i] + 1) +
>                  Y[2, i] * log_theta[2] - lgamma(Y[2, i] + 1) +
>                  log(u_sum[i]);
>  }
>  loglik <- sum(loglik_el) - n*theta_sum;
>  increment_log_prob(loglik);
> }
>  ", file="mvpois.stan")
>
>
>
>
> # estimate parameters
> library(rstan)
> d <- list(Y=Y, n=n, length_u=length_u, u=u, u_mat=u_mat, which_n=which_n)
> init <- stan("mvpois.stan", data = d, chains=0)
> mod <- stan(fit=init,
>            data=d,
>            iter=2000, chains=3,

>
>
>
>

>      )
>
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Another WAIC question (time series?)
messages.body_plain:
My 2 cents: It seems as if Leave-One-Out cross-validation (which WAIC approximates) presupposes that an observation can be left out "at random", i.e. it perhaps depends on the index of the observation but the indices are exchangeable. And exchangeability does not hold with time-series data. A more general approach might be for one observation (at a time) to be considered missing, as opposed to left out. Then estimate the missing observation, along with the other unknowns, compare the posterior distribution of the missing observation to the actual data point, do that for all observations that you have, and average. In that case, it would be pretty explicit that we are talking about ability to predict a missing value among existing groups, rather than predicting a set of values for a new group. But it is not clear to me whether WAIC converges to that. So, if possible, I guess I would try to brute force the cross-validation, treating one observation at a time as missing.

Ben

OK, I see what you're doing in terms of model.

Your generated quantities block is performing a posterior
predictive simulation.  What I was writing was more like
a cross-validation where you fit on earlier data and
then look at the fitted log probability function for new
data.

You could generalize to predict more than just one time
and continue the time series.

For simulation, you could also put the y_next_pred in the model and
sample them all jointly.  This would only be motivated by a more
complex model --- if possible, it's much much more efficient,
both computationally per iteration and statistically in terms of
effective sample size, to do it using RNGs.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] warmup (& convergence)
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] warmup (& convergence)
messages.body_plain:
We've discussed this kind of thing at length before
and when we build in the functionality to allow restarting,
it should be much easier to experiment with.  Then when we have
a method that works, we can implement it.  We're all ears if
you have concrete suggestions.

Let me summarize the discussion so far.

The target of warmup is to

  1. find the high volume mass of the posterior, i.e., get
     our first effective sample, and

  2. estimate the step size (time discretization) and mass
     matrix (Euclidean metric).

We know we've done (1) and (2) well when we are sampling well in
terms of effective samples per iteration.

We have the chicken and egg problem of needing a good step size and
mass matrix (2) before we can effectively find the high volume mass
of the posterior (1), but we need to find the high volume mass of the
posterior (1) before we can effectively estimate step size (2).

The problem with evaluating our mixing-well criterion is that we don't
know what's optimal.  The only way to evaluate that is to do more
adaptation and see if it changes anything.

So what we tend to do now is just be conservative in how long warmup
runs (half total run time), and to suggest continuing to double the
overall number of iterations until you have a high enough n_eff.  At
most this is going to cause something like a 50% inefficiency versus
optimal tuning.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Clarification about Wishart/inv-Wishart distributions in Stan
messages.body_plain:
We have a discussion of our preferred priors, which aren't
conjugate, in the manual chapter on regression.

Doubly cool --- I just saw the latest BDA added the LKJ
correlation density!

More inline on Wishart/inverse Wishart, but I'd really urge
you to read the above.  And then read the paper by Goodrich et al.
that we cite that compares Wishart, inverse Wishart, and the LKJ
priors we recommend.

> On Jan 12, 2015, at 3:29 PM, Christopher Candelaria <chris.ca...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I am in the process of converting a longitudinal model of student performance from WinBUGS to Stan. I am confused about the specification of a Wishart prior in Stan. I reference the "Jaws: repeated measures analysis of variance" example, as it helps point to my source of confusion.
>
> When using BUGS, I know that you specify distributions in terms of precision and not variance. In a multivariate model, this means that you would specify the inverse of the covariance matrix, rather than the covariance matrix. This is how the Jaws example is coded in BUGS: http://www.openbugs.net/Examples/Jaws.html. The model is multivariate normal, and it is distributed with mean vector m and precision matrix W.

Correct.  Stan lets you do it either way.

> The Jaws example was coded into Stan (https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/bugs_examples/vol2/jaws/jaws.stan), where you can specify a multivariate normal distribution in terms of a mean vector and the covariance matrix. In the Jaws example, the covariance matrix is called Sigma.
>
> The Stan model code (excerpt) is as follows:
>
> model {
>   beta0 ~ normal(0, 32);
>   beta1 ~ normal(0, 32);
>   Sigma ~ inv_wishart(4, S); //Relevant part for this post
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     Y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma); //Relevant part for this post
> }
>
> In the example above, Sigma is distributed "inverse Wishart" with scale matrix S and degrees of freedom 4.

Correct.

> First, I believe an inverse-Wishart distribution was chosen for Sigma because it is the conjugate prior distribution for the multivariate normal covariance matrix, so that makes sense.

That's why BUGS chose it --- it's all they can do.  Our translation
is just attempting to follow their model.

We're going to rewrite all their models with slightly different
priors to correspond to how we think they should be coded.

> However, in a general model, shouldn't S be specified as inverse(S). In the Jaws example, S is an identity matrix, so it does not matter, but for a more general scale matrix, it would matter. Am I right about this? According to BDA, if inverse(Sigma) is distributed Wishart(df, S), then Sigma is distributed Inv-Wishart(df, inverse(S)).

> Perhaps I am confused. What is the intuitive definition of the scale matrix for a Wishart and inv-Wishart distribution in Stan?

Not just you --- these reparameterizations are frustratingly confusing
and we could use some better doc (I'll add a clarification in the next
manual release).

We use a scale (covariance) matrix in both cases in Stan.  That
is, our parameter is S in the BDA notation.  BDA confusingly writes

   Sigma ~ Inv-Wishart(inv(S))

so it's not clear what the parmaeter is.

This is similar to the case for the normal.  BDA, like lots of
texts, writes (as many sources do),

  y ~ N(mu,sigma^2)

but that makes it unclear what the parameter is --- sigma^2 or sigma?
In Stan, we just write

  y ~ normal(mu,sigma)

and make it clear that sigma is the parameter.

> For the BUGS Wishart function, the scale matrix is a guess at the order of magnitude of the COVARIANCE matrix (not the precision matrix) for the variable you are modeling. Is it the case that the inv_wishart(.) sampling statement's scale matrix is a guess at the order of magnitude of the precision matrix?

Look at the expectations in the appendix of BDA.  Translated
to Stan notation for dimension k:

  E[wishart(nu,S)] = nu * S

  E[inv_wishart(nu,S)] = S / (nu - k - 1)

BDA writes inv_wishart(nu,inv(S)) for what we write just
as inv_wishart(nu,S).

You can also try to develop intuitions by thinking about the conjugacy
and the way the Wisharts generalize the gamma distribution.  I'm still not
very good at it.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Clarification about Wishart/inv-Wishart distributions in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Bob, for the prompt reply! I appreciate the clarification.

Would you mind sending me the name of the Goodrich et al. article that you had mentioned. I tried to search for it, but I was not sure I found the right paper.

-Chris

On Monday, January 12, 2015 at 2:26:36 PM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> We have a discussion of our preferred priors, which aren't
> conjugate, in the manual chapter on regression.
>
> Doubly cool --- I just saw the latest BDA added the LKJ
> correlation density!
>
> More inline on Wishart/inverse Wishart, but I'd really urge
> you to read the above.  And then read the paper by Goodrich et al.
> that we cite that compares Wishart, inverse Wishart, and the LKJ
> priors we recommend.
>
> > On Jan 12, 2015, at 3:29 PM, Christopher Candelaria <chris.ca...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I am in the process of converting a longitudinal model of student performance from WinBUGS to Stan. I am confused about the specification of a Wishart prior in Stan. I reference the "Jaws: repeated measures analysis of variance" example, as it helps point to my source of confusion.
> >
> > When using BUGS, I know that you specify distributions in terms of precision and not variance. In a multivariate model, this means that you would specify the inverse of the covariance matrix, rather than the covariance matrix. This is how the Jaws example is coded in BUGS: http://www.openbugs.net/Examples/Jaws.html. The model is multivariate normal, and it is distributed with mean vector m and precision matrix W.
>
> Correct.  Stan lets you do it either way.
>
> > The Jaws example was coded into Stan (https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/bugs_examples/vol2/jaws/jaws.stan), where you can specify a multivariate normal distribution in terms of a mean vector and the covariance matrix. In the Jaws example, the covariance matrix is called Sigma.
> >
> > The Stan model code (excerpt) is as follows:
> >
> > model {
> >   beta0 ~ normal(0, 32);
> >   beta1 ~ normal(0, 32);
> >   Sigma ~ inv_wishart(4, S); //Relevant part for this post
> >   for (n in 1:N)
> >     Y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma); //Relevant part for this post
> > }
> >
> > In the example above, Sigma is distributed "inverse Wishart" with scale matrix S and degrees of freedom 4.
>
> Correct.
>
> > First, I believe an inverse-Wishart distribution was chosen for Sigma because it is the conjugate prior distribution for the multivariate normal covariance matrix, so that makes sense.
>
> That's why BUGS chose it --- it's all they can do.  Our translation
> is just attempting to follow their model.
>
> We're going to rewrite all their models with slightly different
> priors to correspond to how we think they should be coded.
>
> > However, in a general model, shouldn't S be specified as inverse(S). In the Jaws example, S is an identity matrix, so it does not matter, but for a more general scale matrix, it would matter. Am I right about this? According to BDA, if inverse(Sigma) is distributed Wishart(df, S), then Sigma is distributed Inv-Wishart(df, inverse(S)).
>
>
> > Perhaps I am confused. What is the intuitive definition of the scale matrix for a Wishart and inv-Wishart distribution in Stan?
>
> Not just you --- these reparameterizations are frustratingly confusing
> and we could use some better doc (I'll add a clarification in the next
> manual release).
>
> We use a scale (covariance) matrix in both cases in Stan.  That
> is, our parameter is S in the BDA notation.  BDA confusingly writes
>
>    Sigma ~ Inv-Wishart(inv(S))
>
> so it's not clear what the parmaeter is.
>
> This is similar to the case for the normal.  BDA, like lots of
> texts, writes (as many sources do),
>
>   y ~ N(mu,sigma^2)
>
> but that makes it unclear what the parameter is --- sigma^2 or sigma?
> In Stan, we just write
>
>   y ~ normal(mu,sigma)
>
> and make it clear that sigma is the parameter.
>
>
> > For the BUGS Wishart function, the scale matrix is a guess at the order of magnitude of the COVARIANCE matrix (not the precision matrix) for the variable you are modeling. Is it the case that the inv_wishart(.) sampling statement's scale matrix is a guess at the order of magnitude of the precision matrix?
>
> Look at the expectations in the appendix of BDA.  Translated
> to Stan notation for dimension k:
>
>   E[wishart(nu,S)] = nu * S
>
>   E[inv_wishart(nu,S)] = S / (nu - k - 1)
>
> BDA writes inv_wishart(nu,inv(S)) for what we write just
> as inv_wishart(nu,S).
>
> You can also try to develop intuitions by thinking about the conjugacy
> and the way the Wisharts generalize the gamma distribution.  I'm still not
> very good at it.
>
> - Bob
>

> Stan
