Hope, yes. Success, maybe. The sparse / dense distinction isn't that useful because Stan doesn't have sparse operations natively. But a few things will help:
Don't use a multivariate normal distribution with a diagonal covariance matrix; equivalently, use a vector of univariate normals that are independent conditional on the parameters
For unknowns, use the Matt trick. For example, make b be a transformed parameter that is equal to sqrt(sigma2b) * b_z and specify b_z ~ normal(0,1) in the model block. Also, if you want, you can parameterize the model in terms of standard deviations rather than variances to avoid taking the sqrt. Same thing for m I guess.
For a, use the multivariate Matt trick: a <- sqrt(sigma2a*(1-w)) * (L * a_z) where L is the Cholesky factor of A (which I assume is fixed? If so, it need only be calculated once.) and to_vector(a_z) ~ normal(0,1).
Post again if you encounter any issues.

Ben

> My 2 cents: It seems as if Leave-One-Out cross-validation (which WAIC approximates) presupposes that an observation can be left out "at random", i.e. it perhaps depends on the index of the observation but the indices are exchangeable. And exchangeability does not hold with time-series data. A more general approach might be for one observation (at a time) to be considered missing, as opposed to left out. Then estimate the missing observation, along with the other unknowns, compare the posterior distribution of the missing observation to the actual data point, do that for all observations that you have, and average. In that case, it would be pretty explicit that we are talking about ability to predict a missing value among existing groups, rather than predicting a set of values for a new group. But it is not clear to me whether WAIC converges to that. So, if possible, I guess I would try to brute force the cross-validation, treating one observation at a time as missing.
>
> Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficient implementation of average predictive comparison (APC, Gelman & Pardoe 2007)?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Efficient implementation of average predictive comparison (APC, Gelman & Pardoe 2007)?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Guido.  I’m cc-ing David Chudzicki because he’s been thinking a lot about this recently and he could have some useful thoughts.
Andrew

> On Jan 13, 2015, at 3:57 PM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Hello,
> I’d appreciate some feedback on the implementation of average predictive comparisons (APC; Gelman & Pardoe 2007) in stan (for now only for non-categorical variables).
>
> ######### if you know APC, jump over this section #######
> Background: In a nutshell, the APC provide an estimate about how much on average a response variable y changes for a one unit change in the predictor variable u, given all other predictor variables v are fixed.
>
>  <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-lLyKFQQolck/VLV81_LV7QI/AAAAAAAB4Ek/7_dQI5j2eY8/s1600/Screen%2BShot%2B2015-01-13%2Bat%2B9.14.46%2BPM.png>
>
> For example, one could examine the effect of the age, number of publications, number of citations,  on the response-variable “has tenure” by running a logistic regression. Calculating APCs for each variable would then  provide an estimate by how many percent the probability to be tenured increases for each age year, number of publications, number of publications, and number of citations, respectively.
>
> Equation 5 in Gelman & Pardoe (2007), describes an algorithm to estimate APCs and uses the following notation:
>
> u, the variable of interest
> v, a vector with the other variables
> theta, the model parameters
> yhat, the model prediction
> n, the number data columns
> S, the number of mcmc sample
>
> to estimate the APC for a variable u as
>
>  <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-vQ0sOErGcUw/VLV9eOA4kwI/AAAAAAAB4Es/QA4NuzSArl8/s1600/Screen%2BShot%2B2015-01-13%2Bat%2B9.17.38%2BPM.png>
>
> here, E(yhat|u_j,v_i,theta_s) is a known function mapping data and parameters to predicted values (e.g. the inverse logit for logistic regressions). w_ij is a Mahalanobis-distance based weight that insuring comparisons u_i-u_j for which v_i and v_j are similar have a greater weight than comparisons u_i-u_j for which v_i and v_j are dissimilar. The term (u_j-u_i) in the denominator has the function to give smaller weight to comparisons with small differences of u, because these are potentially unstable due to noise or incomplete models. Finally, Gelman and Pardoe use the term sign(u_j-u_i) because their algorithm only considers cases where u_i<u_j. Otherwise the denominator and numerator would each sum to zero.
> ################### continue here ##################
>
>
> My APC implementation deviates a bit from a literal implementation of the equation above, and I’d like to know if if my implementation makes sense.
>
> In a nutshell, i prepare pairs for predictive comparisons and weights in the transformed parameters block calculate pair by pair predictive comparisons and their weighted average in the generated quantities block.
>
>
> (I) Generate pairs ui,uj for predictive comparisons
> Because I have too many data rows to make all pair comparisons in a reasonable amount of time, I submit 2 vectors u1s and u2s to stan, which contain row-numbers of the rows to be used to calculate the APCs. Pairs are created from indices in u1s and u2s by combining each u1 in u1s with each u2 in u2s. to avoid the problem of summation to zero, vectors u1s and u2s must be non-overlapping.
>
> In R for example i would create non-overlapping indices as follows:
> uidxs = sample(1:n,500,replace = F)  # sample 500 out of n rows
> u1s = uidxs[1:250]
> u2s = uidxs[251:500]
>
>
> For smaller data sets one could define all pairs in stan by looping only through the lower triangle of the matrix of all possible pairs u_i,u_j:
> for (u1 in 1:(n-1)) {
>  for (u2 in (u1+1):n){
>  ...
>  }
> }
>
> (II) Calculate weights in the transformed data block.
>
> I define weights as w_ij*|u_j-u_i|, where w_ij  is the  Mahalanobis distance based weight proposed by Gelman & Pardoe, and |u_j-u_i| downweights pairs with small differences in u.
> While this also follows Gelman and Pardoe, it still seems a bit ad hoc to me, because one could also omit this second term (when the model is complete and there is not to much noise) or one could take the sqrt(|ui-uj|) of it to avoid overweighting of extreme predictor values. (see also the discussion here: http://www.davidchudzicki.com/predcomps/more-pairs-and-weights.html)
>
>
> Because below I increment the APC comparison by comparison (i.e. I don’t first calculate separate sums for denominator and numerator), my weights have to sum to 1.
>
> stan code:
> (the full model code is attached)
>
> transformed data {
>   // matrix for weights
>   // K = number of predictor variables u (where the intercept is the first predictor)
>   // nus = number of indices first and second part of pair
>   matrix[K-1,nus*nus] weights;
>
>   // matrix for delta_u = u1-u2 to avoid calculating it repeatedly later
>   matrix[K-1,nus*nus] delta_u;
>
>   // matrices to store indices of nonzero u1-u2 differences
>   int<lower=0,upper=N> u1idx[K-1,nus*nus];
>   int<lower=0,upper=N> u2idx[K-1,nus*nus]
>
>   row_vector[K-2] delta_v;
>   matrix[1,1] mhlbd_sq;
>
>   // array to store number of nonzero differences u1-u2
>   int<lower=1> n_pairs[K-1];
>
>   n_pairs <- rep_array(0,K-1);
>   weights <- rep_matrix(0.0, K-1, nus*nus);
>
>
>   for (u in 2:K){ // loop through predictor variables
>     for (u1 in 1:nus){
>       for (u2 in 1:nus){
>         if (x[u1s[u1],u] != x[u2s[u2],u]) {
>           n_pairs[u-1] <- n_pairs[u-1]+1;
>
>           u1idx[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]] <- u1s[u1];
>           u2idx[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]] <- u2s[u2];
>
>           delta_u[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]] <- x[u1s[u1],u] - x[u2s[u2],u];
>
>           // calculate vector delta_v  for Mahalanobis distance
>           // x is the design matrix for the regression, with the intercept in the first column
>          if( u == 2) {
>              delta_v <- sub_row(x,u1s[u1],u+1,K-u) - sub_row(x,u2s[u2],u+1,K-u);
>          } else if (u < K) {
>              delta_v <- append_col(sub_row(x,u1s[u1],2,u-2),sub_row(x,u1s[u1],u+1,K-u)) -
>                         append_col(sub_row(x,u2s[u2],2,u-2),sub_row(x,u2s[u2],u+1,K-u));
>          } else {
>              delta_v <- sub_row(x,u1s[u1],2,u-2) - sub_row(x,u2s[u2],2,u-2);
>          }
>
>
>          // square of mahalabonis distance between vectors v for u1 and u2
>          mhlbd_sq <- to_matrix(delta_v) * iCVs[u-1] * to_matrix(delta_v)';
>
>          // calculate weights from 2 parts: 1) |u1-u2|, 2) square of mahalabonis distance
>          weights[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]] <- fabs(delta_u[u-1,n_pairs[u-1]])*1/(1+mhlbd_sq[1,1]);
>         }
>       }
>     }
>     // normalize weights so that they sum to 0
>     weights[u-1] <- weights[u-1]/sum(weights[u-1]);
>   }
>   print(n_pairs);
> }
>
> (III) Calculate APCs
>
> The basic idea to calculate the APC for a variable u is simple:
> loop through all comparisons,
> calculate a pair’s predictive comparison as (E(y|u_j,v_i,theta_s)-(E_y|u_i,v_i,theta_s))/(u_j-u_i)
> multiply the pair's predictive comparison with its weight (which was prepared in the transformed parameters block)
> increment the APC with the weighted predictive comparison
>
> stan code:
>
> generated quantities {
>   // array to store APCs
>   real APC[K-1];
>   APC <- rep_array(0,K-1);
>
>   for (u in 2:K){ // loop through predictor variables
>     for (k in 1:n_pairs[u-1]) { // loop through pairs with nonzero difference u1-u2
>       // increment            eta=log(mu) of a neg. binomial  * weight
>       APC[u-1] <- APC[u-1] + (exp(eta[u1idx[u-1,k]])-exp(eta[u2idx[u-1,k]]))/delta_u[u-1,k] * weights[u-1,k];
>     }
>   }
> }
>
>
>
> Finally, I am uncertain about the use of matrices vs arrays. I could glean from the stan-reference that arrays have the advantage that values can be returned by reference. On the other hand, I also read that "traversing matrices is more efficient than traversing arrays" (though I haven't checked yet if I am traversing them in the right order). I am not sure what is more relevant here.
> Speed is certainly an issue, because with the current code the sampling phase is slower than the warmup phase.
>
> Best - Guido
>
>
>
>

> --

> For more options, visit https://groups.google.com/d/optout.
> <HZAxNB2RegressionVapc.stan>

I remind my model is the following one:
I have N observations and I would like to do logit regression on them, following a hierarchical model:

hk~ Bernoulli(0.5)
betak | hk  ~ normal(0, hk*sd2 + (1-hk)*sd1) )

Thus: Y| betak,hk  ~ bernoulli_logit ( beta0+ betak* x)

 My original code is this and then i reported my corrections:

        int<lower=0> N;

        real<lower=0> sd2;

            vector[k] betak;
            real<lower=0,upper=1> hk[k];  // i'd like hk to be an integer but i

messages.body_plain:
It's easier to convince people with a working example.
In our experience, marginalizing out discrete parameters leads
to models that fit on the order of 100 to 1000 times faster
than the BUGS/JAGS versions that sample the discrete parameters,
and also have much better robustness and tail behavior.

Having said that, I don't think you can marginalize
in a computationally tractable way in your problem.

You write this

> hk~ Bernoulli(0.5)
> betak | hk  ~ normal(0, hk*sd2 + (1-hk)*sd1) )

but then translate as:

>      beta0 ~ normal(0,0.00001);

Stan uses std-dev as the parameter for normal, not precision,
so this is probably the wrong scale for your problem.  I'd recommend
tighter priors --- there are sections in the manual on recommended
priors in the regression chapter.

But the real problem is here:

>      for( j in 1:k){
>
>            hk[j]~ bernoulli(0.5);   // here, it's the big problem
>
>             betak[j] ~ normal(0, hk*sd2 + (1-hk)*sd1) );
>                       }
>         for(n in 1:N)
>                 y[n]~bernoulli_logit((beta0+ betak* x[n]))
>

I'm assuming you meant x[n] * betak (row vector * vector),
which produces a scalar.   First, write out the joint
density including the discrete parameter:

  p(hk,betak,y)
    =  PROD_j (  bernoulli(hk[j] | 0.5)
                 * normal(betak[j] | hk[j]*sd2 + (1-hk)* sd1) )
       * PROD_n bernoulli_logit(y[n] | beta0 + x[n] * betak)

And then write out the margianlization:

 p(betak,y) = SUM_hk p(hk) * p(betak,y|hk)

where the sum is over all 2^k configurations of hk.  There's no
way to factor that 2^k down the way the examples are in the manual
because the likelihood isn't factored along with the marginalization.

What you want is something that looks like this:

  SUM_{j in 1:k} SUM_{hk[j] in 0:1} p(hk[j]) * p(...|hk[j])

The only way your problem will work in Stan is if 2^k is not too large (on
the order of tens or hundreds rather than thousands or millions).
Then you can do the explicit summation, though it's not going to be pretty
code-wise.

- Bob

>> On Jan 13, 2015, at 3:57 PM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:

>> ...

>> Finally, I am uncertain about the use of matrices vs arrays. I could glean from the stan-reference that arrays have the advantage that values can be returned by reference. On the other hand, I also read that "traversing matrices is more efficient than traversing arrays" (though I haven't checked yet if I am traversing them in the right order). I am not sure what is more relevant here.
>> Speed is certainly an issue, because with the current code the sampling phase is slower than the warmup phase.
>>

The matrix/vector decision is a fairly minor one in terms of speed
in most cases.

Matrices are stored column major, so you want this order
for speed:

  for (n in 1:N)
    for (m in 1:M)
       ... do something with x[m,n] ...

If you need to pull a row out of a matrix and use it for something,
it's better to use an array of row vectors (or just an array of vectors
if you'd otherwise need to transform).

- Bob

> > ## Cholesky, A=LL' (practically dense as well)
> > (L <- t(chol(A)))

> [1,]  1.0  0.0 0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000
> [2,]  0.0  1.0 0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000
> [3,]  0.5  0.5 0.7071068 0.0000000 0.0000000
> [4,]  0.5  0.5 0.0000000 0.7071068 0.0000000
> [5,]  0.5  0.5 0.3535534 0.3535534 0.7071068
>
> ​So the question is now if it is computationally better to define:
>
> A) "conditional way"
>
> a[1]​ <- normal(0, sqrt(sigma2a))
> a[2] <- normal(0, sqrt(sigma2a))
> a[
> ​3
> ] <-
> ​
> normal(0.5*(a[1]+a[2]), sqrt(0.5*sigma2a))
> a[
> 4
> ] <-
> ​
> normal(0.5*(a[1]+a[2]), sqrt(0.5*sigma2a))
> a[
> 5
> ] <-
> ​
> normal(0.5*(a[
> ​3
> ]+a[
> ​4
> ]),
> ​​
> sqrt(
> ​0.5*​
> sigma2a))
>
> ​or
>
> B) "marginal way"
>
> to_vector(a_z) ~ normal(0,1)
> a <- L * a_z​ * sqrt(sigma2a)

First and foremost, it is important to define the model according to your theory; it is only among logically equivalent specifications does computationally efficiency become a consideration. In this case, your "conditional way" is logically different from your "marginal way" unless you impose the restriction that L[2,1] and L[4,3] are both zero. So if L is fixed, then I would say construct an L in R with those two exclusion restrictions, pass it to Stan, and do it the "marginal way".

The "conditional way" is valid (aside from a typo: it should be a[i] ~ normal(...) rather than <- ) because of the DAG structure but entails nonconstant prior dependence among the elements of a (and on sigma2a) which can make it (a bit) more difficult for HMC to sample efficiently. By making a_z primitive (and iid standard normal), you (usually) define a better geometry for the HMC engine to move through.

Ben

On Tuesday, January 13, 2015 at 11:59:33 PM UTC+2, Jonah wrote:
> Thanks Ben and Bob, really appreciate it.
>
> I'll give those ideas a try.

> On Monday, January 12, 2015 at 12:15:57 PM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > My 2 cents: It seems as if Leave-One-Out cross-validation (which WAIC approximates) presupposes that an observation can be left out "at random", i.e. it perhaps depends on the index of the observation but the indices are exchangeable. And exchangeability does not hold with time-series data. A more general approach might be for one observation (at a time) to be considered missing, as opposed to left out. Then estimate the missing observation, along with the other unknowns, compare the posterior distribution of the missing observation to the actual data point, do that for all observations that you have, and average. In that case, it would be pretty explicit that we are talking about ability to predict a missing value among existing groups, rather than predicting a set of values for a new group. But it is not clear to me whether WAIC converges to that. So, if possible, I guess I would try to brute force the cross-validation, treating one observation at a time as missing.
> >
> > Ben

I am using a variety of user-defined functions in my Stan models and I don't quite trust my ability to write bug-free code... so I've taken to copying functions to R and modifying the syntax so that I can test the functions independent of the model.  It would be nice to just use Rcpp and some wrapping code to turn the Stan functions from the .cpp file (after parsing, pre-compilation) into functions callable from R.  That would make ti possible to run/test them from R.  My question is:

1) Has anyone done it?  I I have not been able to find any examples.
2) Are there any known barriers to doing this?  I have also not seen any discussion of this.

I'm interested in doing the wrapping so I'm just trying to save myself some time and grief by checking first.

Thanks!

Krzysztof

messages.body_plain:
The functions are generated C++ in the namespace
<model name>_namespace.

So the question is how to wrap that in Rcpp.

We've been thinking we need something like a unit
testing framework for just this reason.  There aren't
many tools for developing models modularly out of
components, and I think that's a huge bottleneck for
writing complex Stan programs.

- Bob

> On Jan 14, 2015, at 2:26 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:

Yes, and I have to say the dev team's split on whether to
allow this kind of thing or not.

The perceived problem is that our users understand stats
and probability, but not necessarily HMC-based computation.
So what can make sense mathematically can kill the performance
of the sampler.

This would be another argument for some data-only operations.
Right now, there are a couple places where expressions have to
be data only:  some of the args to the ODE solver, and the
size declarations for matrices and arrays.

- Bob

I couldn't parse that all out into a question.
Was there a syntax error you're still dealing with?

The information messages aren't errors --- just issues with
floating point arithmetic that usually resolve themselves during
warmup if the model's well formulated.

The problem you're having is likely this:

> beta~ normal(0.0,sqrt((tau[j]-1)/(tau[j]*a2)));

Because you don't constrain tau in any way.  You need
to make sure a2 > 0 and tau > 1 for this to make sense,
but you have left them unconstrained:

> parameters{
>
>                                                real beta0;
>
>                                                vector[p] beta;
>
>                                                vector[p] tau;
>
>                                                real a1;
>
>                                                real a2;

You need to declare with constraints:

  vector<lower=1>[p] tau;
  vector<lower=0> a1;

There may be other problems, but you need to take care of this first.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Jan 15, 2015, at 3:29 PM, Luke Itiny <luke...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you very much, Bob!!
>
> I forgot those constraints.
> I've corrected my code but I have the same type of warning(at bottom).
> Should I regard these informational messages as a wrong formulation of the model?

No, it usually just means that the step size is too large when following
the gradient.  Stan adapts step size and mass matrix during warmup.
Too small a step means things go too slowly and too large a step means
these kinds of errors and Metropolis rejections, so we try to find the
middle ground.

If you only get a few of these during warmup, it's OK.  If they
persist, there's a problem with the model.

You can try lowering initial step size, which often causes them to
go away.

It's probably in the standard deviation being able to be very tiny.
Where is it at when Stan's done sampling?  Does n_eff look OK?

Is it possible to pickle a fitted pystan model?

Following the example on this page <http://pystan.readthedocs.org/en/latest/avoiding_recompilation.html>, I was able to pickle a compiled model (and then unpickle it for later use), but I can't tell for sure if you can pickle a fitted model, too.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Noah,

There are model objects and fit objects. Model objects are picklable.
Pickling them is well-tested.

For fit objects, the best strategy is to pickle the output of the
fit, so `pickle.dump(fit.extract(), f)`.

That said, it is possible to pickle the entire fit object with the
caveat that you *must* have the associated model object available in the
current environment. So you could unpickle the model object and only
then unpickle the fit object. (The plan is to clean up this problem in
Stan 3.0.)

Best wishes,

Allen

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Large ridge regression/hierarchical like model
messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

I have done some changes to my test case of the ridge regression model. I have now 1) used fixed seed so that all test start from the same starting point (if I got the stan() R documentation right) to avoid different startup for warmup, 2) I have also extended sampling period to get more constant timings, and 3) tried two cases with the same number of covariates (nM=1000), but only a few records (nY=50) or "lots" of records (nY=5000) to contrast what happens when signal to noise ratio changes. The model codes A-D are the same as posted before with varying changes as suggested by Ben. The summary is, that, yes, the proposed changes to the code help to get larger ESS/s when signal to noise is low, but there is not much difference when signal is quite strong. I think this makes sense. I am only puzzled why the D case gave smaller ESS/s than the C case with low signal to noise ratio. Looks like increment_log_prob(-0.5 * dot_self(m_z)) seems to be more expensive than m_z ~ normal(0, 1).

If I may I would suggest to try to get ESS/s into the summary (all the components are already there printed out and a bit of a pain to collect), to facilitate making such comparisons easily.

Thanks!

gg

# A nY=50, nM=1000
warm <- c( 21.38,  21.22, 19.12,  22.43)
samp <- c(177.15, 116.74, 251.5, 129.98)

> On Jan 16, 2015, at 8:12 AM, Gregor Gorjanc <gregor....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi again,
>
> I have done some changes to my test case of the ridge regression model. I have now 1) used fixed seed so that all test start from the same starting point (if I got the stan() R documentation right) to avoid different startup for warmup, 2) I have also extended sampling period to get more constant timings, and 3) tried two cases with the same number of covariates (nM=1000), but only a few records (nY=50) or "lots" of records (nY=5000) to contrast what happens when signal to noise ratio changes. The model codes A-D are the same as posted before with varying changes as suggested by Ben. The summary is, that, yes, the proposed changes to the code help to get larger ESS/s when signal to noise is low, but there is not much difference when signal is quite strong.

See the Betancourt and Girolami arXiv paper on HMC for hierarchical
models or some of its antecedents.

> I think this makes sense. I am only puzzled why the D case gave smaller ESS/s than the C case with low signal to noise ratio. Looks like increment_log_prob(-0.5 * dot_self(m_z)) seems to be more expensive than m_z ~ normal(0, 1).
>
> If I may I would suggest to try to get ESS/s into the summary (all the components are already there printed out and a bit of a pain to collect), to facilitate making such comparisons easily.
>

There's an issue tracker for RStan where you can submit feature
requests.

We currently print out ESS/s in CmdStan, but it excludes warmup
time --- it's just measuring the marginal ESS/s once you're
sampling.

We'll be making a pass soon through all the interfaces to try
to bring them all in line, which will probably involve combining
all of their features.

- Bob

On Friday, January 16, 2015 at 7:24:11 PM UTC-5, Anders Holden wrote:
> What is the best way of summing a set of values by group, like the function tapply in R

There isn't a good way. The least bad way is to pass an integer vector or starting indices and group sizes and then use segment(). Like

for(g in 1:groups) sumEV[g] <- sum(segment(EV, starts[g], sizes[g]));

This presumes the observations are sorted by group.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
When installing rstan on a cluster, how should one go about choosing the number of cores to use for the build (in the line Sys.setenv(MAKEFLAGS = "-j4")? If each node in the cluster has 16 cores, does it make sense to set the value to 16? What if a user wants to run stan across multiple nodes with MPI? Or does it make the most sense to keep the value at 4 in any case, since most people will be running no more than 4 chains in parallel anyway? I would really appreciate any advice on this setting.

Thanks,
John

messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, January 18, 2015 at 12:07:23 PM UTC-5, John Palmer wrote:
> When installing rstan on a cluster, how should one go about choosing the number of cores to use for the build (in the line Sys.setenv(MAKEFLAGS = "-j4")? If each node in the cluster has 16 cores, does it make sense to set the value to 16? What if a user wants to run stan across multiple nodes with MPI? Or does it make the most sense to keep the value at 4 in any case, since most people will be running no more than 4 chains in parallel anyway? I would really appreciate any advice on this setting.

The numer of cores at build time does not affect the number of cores at run time. And it doesn't take that long to install Stan, so it doesn't really matter whether you do -j4 or -8 or whatever.

I am not aware of any experience with MPI specifically but everyone's cluster is different, so it wouldn't surprise me if someone has done it. What interface(s) to Stan are we considering here? If we are talking RStan, then I would think using parallel::mclapply on one 16 core node would be fine (if you have enough RAM). Stan cannot yet parallelize functions, so the only option is to parallelize chains, and I haven't seen a need for more than 16 chains.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Seems reasonable, but I'm surprised by the decision to create the pairs/weights inside Stan rather than do that step in another language and provide it to Stan as input data. I don't know if that step is slow, but if it is there'd be an advantage to doing it outside Stan and saving it once and for all. Then as you tweak the model, you don't need to do that step again each time you run Stan.

On the other hand, I also read that "traversing matrices is more efficient than traversing arrays" (though I haven't checked yet if I am traversing them in the right order). I am not sure what is more relevant here.
> >> Speed is certainly an issue, because with the current code the sampling phase is slower than the warmup phase.
> >>
>
> The matrix/vector decision is a fairly minor one in terms of speed
> in most cases.
>
> Matrices are stored column major, so you want this order
> for speed:
>
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     for (m in 1:M)
>        ... do something with x[m,n] ...
>
> If you need to pull a row out of a matrix and use it for something,
> it's better to use an array of row vectors (or just an array of vectors
> if you'd otherwise need to transform).
>
> - Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] understanding profiling Stan
messages.body_plain:
If addition's taking 15% of your time, you're probably
in very good shape.

> On Jan 18, 2015, at 5:42 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I've been developing some models which make heavy use of functions to calculate splines and indexes for convenience, and before elaborating things any further, I attached Oprofile to a running model to see if I had some performance-related no-no's.  I did notice that my spline functions show up (part of the Oprofile output below) which suggests I might want to move the weight calculations out when possible (spline weights can be precalculated for this model, as can all the indexes).  It's nice to see that the Oprofile output is so helpful.

Everything that can be calculated in transformed
data should be calculated in transformed data.
Same for generated quantities.

> add_vv_vari is big---that seems to be from the reverse mode auto-diff for the addition operator and there's not much to do about it for splines or linear models...

The biggest thing to do is replace sequences of +=
operations with a vector sum.  It's more efficient in
autodiff as it only needs a single virtual function
call and guarantees much more memory locality in the
derivative calcs.

> same goes for divide_vd_vari/sq_vari/exp_vari/etc... except that some of those must be from calculating spline weights (?) Other than the prominence of the spline functions, this seems to square with the general view that most of the time is spent calculating gradients.

Some of these come with transforms.  For instance, exp_vari
comes in through the Jacobian for

  parameters {
    real<lower=0> sigma;

which itself needs to be differentiated.  Sometimes you can
reparameterize directly with unconstrained variables.  We support
that in some cases directly with probability functions like
poisson_log and bernoulli_logit.

If the subtract_vd and divide_vd are coming from probability functions like

  y ~ normal(0,1);

then they could probably be sped up if we had a centered_normal
and unit_normal.

> My trying-to-understand-Stan questions: for someone more familiar with profiling Stan---are there any additional lessons here for the model? Are other forms of the Oprofile output more useful for figuring this out?
>

I think that looks pretty good!  The time's all being
spent in autodiff derivative propagatins (the chain()
methods), which is what we'd expect.

- Bob

messages.subject: infer binary latent variables with STAN?
messages.subject_clean: infer binary latent variables with STAN?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan users and developers,

Hello. We are now working on a model (see below), where, for each object k, we wished to determine whether or not the object has a defect based on two attributes we measured for each object in our analysis (norm_Aff[k], and Acc[k], see below, highlighted in red).

The variable norm_Aff[k] is the primary determinant and the Acc[k] is more secondary for the product defectiveness (greater values, better production quality), so in our model we made Acc as part of the prior for the binary latent variable delta[k], indicating whether or not one object is defective (0 is defective)

In our study, we examined almost 10 millions of the objects,  and tested the model below using OpenBugs - it ran well well on a very small dataset (~100-500 objects), and gave very reasonable output, but the program took very long for the whole dataset, and eventually died. We have a very powerful cluster machine to do this computation, so I guess the problem should not be caused by memory/disk overflow etc.

My colleagues strongly recommended us to try STAN, as it is written in C and the sampling algorithms are more efficient than BUGs, so we were just wondering if STAN could handle this situation. We noticed in previous discussion that STAN might not directly accept discrete latent variables, and I am not sure if it is still the case. In our studies, a binary latent switch is extremely important in our modeling, so is there any workaround for this?

Thank you very much for your kind help, and we really appreciate it!!

Jorlen

model <- function() {
        for (k in 1:K){
                norm_Aff[k] ~ dnorm(mu[k], tau)
                mu[k] <- mu0 + w1*delta[k]
                delta[k] ~ dbern(p[k])
                p[k] <- Acc[k]*alpha
        }
        mu0 ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)
        alpha ~ dbeta(1,1)
        w1 ~ dgamma(0.01,0.01)
        tau~dgamma(0.01,0.01)
}

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, January 21, 2015 at 2:30:34 AM UTC-5, Jorlen Li wrote:
> We noticed in previous discussion that STAN might not directly accept discrete latent variables, and I am not sure if it is still the case. In our studies, a binary latent switch is extremely important in our modeling, so is there any workaround for this?

In general, HMC requires derivatives to generate proposals for the unknowns and discrete unknowns are not differentiable. However, it is often possible to at least write down a conceptually equivalent model that only has continuous unknowns. In your case, I think you want to express your posterior distribution

f(delta, mu0, alpha, w1, tau | data)

as the product over k of

f(mu0, alpha, w1, tau | data, delta[k] = 0) * Pr(delta[k] = 0 | data) +
f(mu0, alpha, w1, tau | data, delta[k] = 1) * Pr(delta[k] = 1 | data)

So, basically express your posterior distribution as a mixture of two posterior distributions with a Bernoulli mixing distribution. This is going to be a bit tedious because you have to loop over k and express the two components for each observation. Then, in the generated quantities block, you could draw from the posterior predictive distribution of the latent unknowns given the data.

Look in Chapter 9 (Finite Mixtures) of the Stan manual for more details and examples of how to do this.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I added a note to the latest manual issue to fix the doc.

The to_vector is just because we don't allow matrix arguments
to univariate densities because of issues in trying to interpret
what matching shapes mean.  If there is more than one vector or
container argument, they all must be the same size.

The problem you're having is that all the dimensions have to line
up.

Problem 1:  You're trying to initialize K x D and you only
want to initialize (K-1) x D, because you initialize the parameter,
not the transformed thing.

Problem 2:  beta * xmat[n] dimensions won't line up, because
beta is K x D and xmat[n] is K x 1.  We don't test sizes at
compile time, which is why the model compiles.  What you want
is to declare xmat as an array of row vectors and use

  xmat[n] * beta

or you want to declare beta as being D x K instead of D x K
and fix everything else.

Problem 3:  You don't want to apply softmax directly.  Use
the appropriate categorical, which is more efficient and
arithmetically stable,

  y[n] ~ categorical_logit(xmat[n] * beta);

Then you can vectorize and if xmat is declared as a matrix,
just use

  y ~ categorical_logit(xmat * beta);

which is the most stable and efficient way to code this.

Problem 4:  Did you want to append a row of 1 rather than 0?  The
row of 0 isn't going to do much in a multiplication.  Also, it's
inefficient to do it this way as opposed to the way you originally wrote it.

- Bob

> >
> > f(delta, mu0, alpha, w1, tau | data)
> >
> > as the product over k of
> >
> > f(mu0, alpha, w1, tau | data, delta[k] = 0) * Pr(delta[k] = 0 | data) +
> > f(mu0, alpha, w1, tau | data, delta[k] = 1) * Pr(delta[k] = 1 | data)
> >
> > So, basically express your posterior distribution as a mixture of two posterior distributions with a Bernoulli mixing distribution. This is going to be a bit tedious because you have to loop over k and express the two components for each observation. Then, in the generated quantities block, you could draw from the posterior predictive distribution of the latent unknowns given the data.
> >
> > Look in Chapter 9 (Finite Mixtures) of the Stan manual for more details and examples of how to do this.
> >
> > Ben

messages.body_plain:
There's no way to predict speed from size alone (even the size
of data plus size of parameters and knowledge of sparsity of data).
The form of the model along with the specific data set will determine
how well-behaved the posterior will be.

But even for simple models, MCMC won't be fast for 10M observations.
You might not be able to fit something that large for a complex
model using MCMC.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan in the Juliabox
messages.body_plain:
Andrew,

Stan is installed and available for everyone on JuliaBox, so it is completely ready to go. To use JuliaBox you do need a JuliaBox account.

If you don’t have a JuliaBox account yet, an email to Viral (cc-ed) I believe is the easiest way to set this up. Maybe it is also possible to create a general demo account shared for Stan-related demo purposes, but I’m not sure if this is acceptable to JuliaBox.org <http://JuliaBox.org>.

If you have a JuliaBox account, just log in using the browser. Below I have attached 2 example notebooks, including the EightSchools example. The Bernoulli example is also on Stan.jl on Github.

JuliaBox gives you your own file space to store Julia and Stan scripts. Once you log in, you can upload the 2 example files (using the ‘Files’ menu item) and open them from the 'IJulia' menu item (by clicking one of the files that you have just uploaded).

I don’t know how familiar you are with Notebook-like interfaces, so it is difficult to gauge exactly how to best help setting it up and get you going, but I’m more than happy to help out.

Regards,
Rob J. Goedman
goe...@mac.com

>                                              ^

The code that generated this message:

> data {
>   int<lower=2> C;   # categories of y

>   int<lower=0> N;   # observations

Re problem 4: If the coefficients are log-odds, I think I would want to constrain coefficients for the base category to zero, no?

Thanks for your quick and very helpful responses. Stan is a beautiful thing.

messages.body_plain:
> On Jan 21, 2015, at 11:27 PM, Rick Farouni <rfar...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> Let's say I want to estimate K threshold vectors for an ordered logistic model and I would like to estimate them hierarchically. My questions are the following:
>
> 1) If I re-parameterize the Stan model to make it run more efficiently, which of the three parameter vectors  (tau_raw[K], mu_tau_unif, tau[K]) in the reparameterized model do I need to specify as an ordered vector?

tau --- that's the one that's the parameter to the ordered_logistic().

I'm not sure the reparameterization will be more efficient, though you
can always test it.  Some others on the list might have a better idea
in principle.

> 2) Is there a difference between the two versions of the model with respect to how the Stan's model compiler transforms the constrained ordered vectors into an unconstrained vectors before sampling?

Yes.  There's a chapter in the manual that explains the transforms
in detail, but the general idea is that lower-bounds lead to log transforms
(exp inverse transforms in practice) and lower and upper bounds lead
to logit (inverse logit in practice) transforms.

> 3) For the sake of convenience, I put a normal prior of tau, but am I allowed to put such a prior on set of ordered vectors?

Yes, you can do that.  Like every other sampling statement,
it just adds terms to the log density.  It basically winds
up providing a similar prior to having a bunch of independent
normals that get sorted (though that's not going on under the hood).

> Does Stan reject samples that do not meet the constraint?

Not quite.  Because tau is a parameter declared as ordered[C-1],
Stan will use (C - 1) unconstrained parameters, all but the first
of which are log transformed differences from the previous parameter.

- Bob

> Here is a stripped-down version of the model:
>
> data {
>   int<lower=0> K; // number of items
>   int<lower=0> N; // number of responses
>   int<lower=1,upper=K> kk[N];   // item index for response n
>   int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];    // data vector
>   int<lower=2> C;// number of response categories (e.g. 5)
> }
> parameters {
>   ordered[C-1] tau[K];// K threshold vectors, each of dimension C-1
>   vector[C-1] mu_tau; // mean vector for thresholds
>   vector<lower=0>[C-1] sigma_tau; //scale
> }
>
>
> model {
> //hyperpriors
> mu_tau~cauchy(0,5)
> sigma_tau~cauchy(0,3)
> //prior
>   for(k in 1:K){
>     for (i in 1:(C-1))
>       tau[k][i]~normal(mu_tau[i],sigma_tau[i]);
>            }
> //the likelihood
>   for (n in 1:N)
>   y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(.....,tau[kk[n]]);
>
>
> }
>
>
> And here is the re-parameterized model:
>
> parameters {
>   ordered[C-1] tau_raw[K];// K threshold vectors, each of dimension C-1
>   ordered<lower=-pi()/2,upper=pi()/2>[C-1] mu_tau_unif; // mean vector for thresholds
>   vector<lower=0,upper=pi()/2>[C-1] sigma_tau_unif;
> }
>
>
> transformed parameters {
>   ordered[C-1] tau[K];// K threshold vectors, each of dimension C-1
>   ordered<lower=-pi()/2,upper=pi()/2>[C-1] mu_tau; // mean vector for thresholds
>   vector<lower=0,upper=pi()/2>[C-1] sigma_tau;
>
>   mu_tau <-5*tan(mu_tau_unif);          //reparameterization: mu_tau~cauchy(0,3)
>   sigma_tau <-3*tan(sigma_tau_unif);      //reparameterization: sigma_tau~half-cauchy(0,3)
>   for(k in 1:K){
>      tau[k]<-mu_tau+sigma_tau .*tau_raw[k];} //reparameterization: tau[k]~normal(mu_tau,sigma_tau)
> }
>
>
> model {
> /* implicit  hyperpriors
> * mu_tau_unif ~ uniform(-pi/2,pi/2):implies the  hyperprior mu_tau~cauchy(0,5)
> */ sigma_tau_unif ~ uniform(0,pi/2): implies the  hyperprior sigma_tau~cauchy(0,3)
>
> //prior
> for(k in 1:K){
>     tau_raw[k]~normal(0,1);} //implies the hierarchical prior tau[k]~multi_normal(mu_tau,diag(sigma_tau))
>
>
> //the likelihood
>   for (n in 1:N)
>   y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(.....,tau[kk[n]]);
>
>
> }
>
>
> Thanks in advance,
>
>

Argh.  That was my bad suggestion.  We haven't fully generalized
our multivariate distributions like categorical_logit (it's not
quite multivariate, but takes a vector parameter) to allow vectors
of parameters.  So it can take an array of outcomes, but only allows
a single parameter.

I was going to fast and assuming xmat * beta was just a vector.

xmat * beta wouldn't have worked anyway, because the dimensions
don't line up (xmat is N x K and beta is C x K, so they can't
be multiplied without transposing one of them).

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Ordered Vectors, Prior Distributions, and Efficient Reparametrization
messages.body_plain:
> On Jan 22, 2015, at 2:55 PM, Rick Farouni <rfar...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
>
> On Thursday, January 22, 2015 at 2:39:26 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>

> > On Jan 21, 2015, at 11:27 PM, Rick Farouni <rfar...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi,
> >
> > Let's say I want to estimate K threshold vectors for an ordered logistic model and I would like to estimate them hierarchically. My questions are the following:
> >
> > 1) If I re-parameterize the Stan model to make it run more efficiently, which of the three parameter vectors  (tau_raw[K], mu_tau_unif, tau[K]) in the reparameterized model do I need to specify as an ordered vector?
>
> tau --- that's the one that's the parameter to the ordered_logistic().
>

> But in the FAQ, Ben Goodrich says that "the restrictions on the support of a transformed parameter in the transformed parameters {} block do not affect the sampling because Stan samples from the space of the parameters" . In the reparamterized model, tau is in the transformed parameters block.

It doesn't technically need to be declared as ordered if it's
in the transformed parameters block --- the ordered declaration will
just do error checking after the transformed params are defined.

It's then up to you to make sure that the transformed parameter really
is ordered, or you'll get rejections.  You don't want rejections of
this kind as they can cause the sampler to devolve to an inefficient
random walk.  You want support over all the legal *parameter*
values --- that is, any value of the parameters matching the constraint
should not be rejected elsewhere or the sampler will devolve.

> I'm not sure the reparameterization will be more efficient, though you
> can always test it.  Some others on the list might have a better idea
> in principle.
>
> > 2) Is there a difference between the two versions of the model with respect to how the Stan's model compiler transforms the constrained ordered vectors into an unconstrained vectors before sampling?
>
> Yes.  There's a chapter in the manual that explains the transforms
> in detail, but the general idea is that lower-bounds lead to log transforms
> (exp inverse transforms in practice) and lower and upper bounds lead
> to logit (inverse logit in practice) transforms.

I guess I should come to grips with that.  I knew it was
in there.  The efficiency of some of these transforms can depend
on how much data you have an how much that constrains the posterior.

> > 3) For the sake of convenience, I put a normal prior of tau, but am I allowed to put such a prior on set of ordered vectors?
>
> Yes, you can do that.  Like every other sampling statement,
> it just adds terms to the log density.  It basically winds
> up providing a similar prior to having a bunch of independent
> normals that get sorted (though that's not going on under the hood).
>

> Is there a reference out there that can explain what goes on under the hood?

The manual, but I can summarize.  Every sampling statement:

  y ~ foo(theta);

increments the log density by log foo(y|theta).  Any constrained
parameter increments the log density with the log Jacobian of the
inverse transform.  The transforms we use are all documented.

So if you look at ordering

  ordered[K] c;

Then you have unconstrained params:

  c1,...,cK

which lead to transformed params

  c1, c1 + exp(c2), c1 + exp(c2) + exp(c3), ...

The log Jacobian of the transform is just (c2 + ... + cK).

You can also increment the log density directly using increment_log_prob.

We then just sample from whatever posterior is defined by the density.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for all assistance. The model now runs beautifully--with ~22K observations, 8 predictors, and 4 categorical outcomes, it converges in < 50 iterations, which seems pretty amazing, and it runs at a little under a second per iteration. So it takes about 15 minutes to generate about 1000 samples (3 chains, 50/350). You are welcome to use (and edit) the code as an example, for what it's worth:

> data {
>   int<lower=2> C;   # categories of y
>   int<lower=0> N;   # observations
>   int<lower=1> K;   # variables
>   int<lower=1,upper=C> y[N];    # outcome indicator

>   vector[K] xmat[N];
> }
>
> parameters {
>   matrix[C-1,K] beta_free;
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>   matrix[C,K] beta;
>   for (k in 1:K)
>     beta[1,k] <- 0;
>   for (c in 2:C)
>     for (k in 1:K)
>       beta[c,k] <- beta_free[c-1,k];
> }
>
> model {
>   for (c in 2:C)
>     for (k in 1:K)
>       beta[c,k] ~ normal(0,2);

>   for (n in 1:N)
>     y[n] ~ categorical(softmax(beta * xmat[n]));
> }

You'll note that I borrowed from the Alligators example to constrain parameters for the first outcome to be zero.

Best,
John

messages.body_plain:
I recommend doing half the iterations for warmup and half for samples that you use.  Economizing on warmup isn’t always such an economy.  Or, to put it another way:  If you only need 50 warmup, I think you probably only need 50 for samples.  Or, if you want to be safe and have 350 for samples, I think you should really be safe and have 350 for warmup.

I have no proof on this (it’s an issue I’ve thought about, without success, for about 25 years) but that’s my impression.
A

P.S.  I’m glad the model runs beautifully!

> Jeez you're quick--thanks! I took you to mean that the declaration of b0 should be changed to
>
> > vector[J] b0[C];

vector[J] b0[C] is an array with C elements, each of which is a vector of J elements, i.e. you have an array of C J-vectors. So b0[1] is an entire J-vector, as are b0[2], ..., b0[C]. To refer to the jth element of the cth b0 vector you would then use b0[c,j].

> >
> though I confess I don't know what that statement really means. Anyway, now it's rejected for a different--but perhaps related--reason, with a series of messages like:

> > stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter[1]  is -0.407936:0, but must be > 0!

It's telling you that the scale parameter (sigma) of the normal distribution -- which is constrained to be positive  --  has a negative value.
Is there more to the message that says it's fine if it occurs occasionally? I might be mistaken, but I think if this happens in warmup you should be ok but if it's happening a lot during sampling then something is amiss.

John,

Everything Jonah has said is correct.

sigma_b0_free needs to be lower bound at zero for efficient sampling. It'll work (sometimes) as you've defined it, but what you want to do is replace:
    vector[C-1] sigma_b0_free;

That will transform the underlying parameter so you'll always sample a standard deviation component greater than 0.

This is Stan / C++ is very similar to the R construct of a list of length C where each list element is a numeric vector of length J. So, you could access that in R with

b0[[c]][j]

to obtain the j-th element of the c-th vector. In Stan, it is just

b0[c,j]

or

b0[c][j]

Declare the standard deviations with a positivity constraint

vector<lower=0>[C-1] sigma_b0_free

Then, you would be two steps closer to having it work.

messages.subject: Possible inconsistency in PySTAN utility stan_rdump
messages.subject_clean: Possible inconsistency in PySTAN utility stan_rdump
messages.body_plain:
SUMMARY of a possible issue:
Python implements arrays row-wise, Stan implements arrays column-wise.
This may have been overlooked in https://github.com/stan-dev/pystan/blob/develop/pystan/misc.py .
Direct usage of stan_rdump may lead to unexpected results.

DETAILED description:
Dear STAN community,

I wanted to share some debugging experience - maybe someone will have the same issue.

The data I am using in my STAN program is generated and used by a python script.
To convert python arrays to *.data.R, I am using the functions _dict_to_rdump, stan_rdump
from PyStan utilities (https://github.com/stan-dev/pystan/blob/develop/pystan/misc.py,
further referred to as [1]).

According to CmdStan Interface User's Guide 2.5.0, p. 70, data is stored in the column-major
order.

''... For example,

        y <- structure(c(1,2,3,4,5,6), .Dim = c(2,3))

This defines a 2 × 3 array. Data is stored in column-major order, meaning the values
for y will be as follows.

        y[1,1] = 1         y[1,2] = 3        y[1,3] = 5
        y[2,1] = 2         y[2,2] = 4        y[2,3] = 6
"

Using Python, I would define this array in the following way:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> y = np.asarray([[1,3,5], [2,4,6]])
>>> y
array([[1, 3, 5],
         [2, 4, 6]])

Assume that I want to put this array into *.data.R, so I copy the necessary functions from [1] and call

>>> data = dict( data_y = y )
>>> _dict_to_rdump(data)

As far as I can tell, this data is wrapped to *.data.R in [1, lines 969-971]:

"
     s = tmpl.format(name,
                            ', '.join(str(v) for v in value.flat),
                            ', '.join(str(v) for v in value.shape))
"

In our case, one can check that

>>> y.flat[0]
1
>>> y.flat[1]
3

etc., and

>>> y.shape
(2,3)

 i.e. the flattening of y happens row-wise. Thus, one obtains the following string dumped to *.data.R:

data_y <-
structure(c(1,3,5,2,4,6), .Dim = c(2,3))

That string will be unpacked by STAN in the column-major order, namely (cf. above)

        data_y[1,1] = 1         data_y[1,2] = 5        data_y[1,3] = 4
        data_y[2,1] = 3         data_y[2,2] = 2        data_y[2,3] = 6

which (IMHO) makes it very non-intuitive. I ended up exchanging "value.shape" in [1, line 971] by
'value.shape[::-1]", which leads to

data_y <-
structure(c(1,3,5,2,4,6), .Dim = c(3,2))

unpacked by STAN as

        data_y[1,1] = 1         data_y[1,2] = 2
        data_y[2,1] = 3         data_y[2,2] = 4
        data_y[3,1] = 5         data_y[3,2] = 6

which is not exactly the input array y, but it is the same as transpose(y). This, again, can be corrected
by using 'np.transpose(value)' instead of 'value' in _dict_to_rdump in [1], but I was not sure whether this
can lead to complications for high-dimensional arrays.

Best regards,
Arseniy.

messages.body_plain:
This text from the manual (end of page 30):

> Arrays, on the other hand, should be traversed in row-major (or first-index fastest)
> order.

Seems to contradict this code:

real a[M,N];

for (m in 1:M)
  for (n in 1:N)
... do something with a[m,n] ...

As well as this text:

> The first use of a[m,n] should bring a[m] into memory. Overall, traversing matrices
> is more efficient than traversing arrays.

Isn't this last-index-fastest since a[m] (for all values of n) is brought into memory?

Krzysztof

Hi all,

Here's a Stan model of non-negative matrix factorisation (actually a
bit PLCA-style) intended as a simple model of the type used for music
transcription:
https://gist.github.com/danstowell/151a3b68ceb9c5f4a51f

It works fine on small toy data. I'd just like to ask if the example
could be written better because I ended up doing a couple of inelegant
things:

simplex into a matrix row not into a matrix column;
* iterating over the columns of a matrix to specify them all as
exponential rather than writing a single "~ exponential()" for the
whole lot.

There might be a neater way that I've missed.

Thanks
Dan

only one file cmdStanKit.py is needed.

a simple stan_rdump, avoiding GPL issue
sampling leverages all cores and merges outputs into one file
skip noisy outputs on screen and only show when compiling errors happened.

future roadmap:
add more options to sampling
count several kinds of warnings and decide whether it's serious enough. suspend if any kind of warnings is too many
diagnose workflow

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for sharing the model.  In terms of the model,
what's the motivation for flattening Xnorm and using
a single Dirichlet rather than doing it column or row-wise?

For efficiency:

1.  calculate Xnorm, Wmat and Winitnorm in the transformed
data block.  From what I can tell, they only depend on data.
Then they'll only be calculated once rather than potentially
several times per iteration.  Then all the transposing and
what not is only done once so nothing at all to worry about for
speed.

2.  Rather than iterating over columns a matrix, you can
just do:

  to_vector(H) ~ exponential(Hconc);

We're working on making more direct implementations for this,
but this is the best that's available now.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Like all programming, writing efficient Stan programs
comes down to understanding how they get compiled and executed.

There's a discussion in the arrays and matrices chapter of
the manual that tries to explain those decisions.

There's also a discussion of how code in different blocks
gets executed and when.

The big picture for Stan (both MCMC and optimization)
is that taking gradients is expensive compared
to everything else.  Doing work on simple data types like
vectors is usually a win if it cuts down on work done for
gradients.  So basically anything that can be done to vectorize
a sampling statement (or a function evaluation like normal_log)
is a win.  In the best case, fewer calculations will be done
such as log(sigma) in normal_log(y,mu,sigma) if y and/or mu
are vectors.

Unlike in R or Python, loops themselves aren't the expensive part.
Only when they prevent vectorization of probability functions or
other derivative-involving operations.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
There's a bit more overhead in the transformed parameters
block because the variable gets stored in an array and then
ignored on output if it's not being monitored.  Making it
a local variable in the model avoids any additional copying
and switching.

Plus, as Ben pointed out, you have more options to check
constraints in the transformed parameters block, which can be
expensive for some types like covariance matrices.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] stan and machine learning
messages.body_plain:
If you build the model as a mixture, you can
calculate posterior probabilities for each mixture
component on a per-item basis.  That is, you get a
probabilistic classifier for free.   Is it the
classification aspect of this that you think of as
machine learning?

If there are covariates, the Poissons can have means
estimated by a GLM.

And there's almost always overdispersion in real data,
so you might want to try negative binomial instead (just
be careful about all the parameterizations floating around
the literature and in Stan).

- Bob

I am attaching the stan code. I will try to create some sample simulated data later, if that is useful.

Thanks,

Chris

I am using a relatively new computer cluster to run my model. Here are the details of the system to which I have access :
Two load balanced login nodes
120 general compute nodes with dual socket Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-2650 v2 @ 2.60GHz (8 core/socket); 64 GB 1866 MHz DDR3; 100 GB local SSD
2 "big data" nodes with quad socket Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-4640 @ 2.40GHz (8 core/socket); 1.5 TB RAM; 13 TB local storage
5 GPU nodes with dual socket Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-2640 v2 @ 2.00GHz; 256 GB RAM; 200 GB local storage
2:1 oversubscribed FDR Infiniband network
1 PB Lustre parallel file system for /scratch
Here is the contents of my SBATCH program:

#!/bin/bash
#cvamstan.sbatch, a sample slurm job
#
#all commands that start with SBATCH contain commands that are just used by SLURM for scheduling
#################
#set a job name
#SBATCH --job-name=cvamV04_m_cohort2004_c1
#################
#a file for job output, you can check job progress
#SBATCH --output=cvamV04_m_cohort2004_c1.out
#################
# a file for errors from the job
#SBATCH --error=cvamV04_m_cohort2004_c1.err
#################
#time you think you need; default is one hour
#SBATCH --time=8:00:00
#################
#quality of service; think of it as job priority
#SBATCH --qos=normal
#################
#number of nodes you are requesting
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#################
#memory per node; default is 4000 MB per CPU
#SBATCH --mem=50GB
#################
#task to run per node; each node has 16 cores, "task" is "core" really
#SBATCH --ntasks=4
#don't use --cpus-per-task on this cluster
#################

And here is the command I issue to run cmdstan:
#Chain 1
./cvamV4_4year sample num_samples=15000 num_warmup=3000 save_warmup=0 \

messages.body_plain:
Thanks.  I should've read more closely.

We were torn between embedding more deeply and
by calling CmdStan remotely.  The other big advantage
is that calling it in a separate process can't tank
your Python process!

I appreciate a license that's more liberal than GPL.

I'd be careful about skipping noisy outputs in case they're
needed somewhere for diagnosing an issue.  Maybe a flag to
make output verbose or terse.  We're working on getting
things perfectly silent --- some of the prints got away from
us and we're reeling them back in.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
It helps to write everything out mathematically.
I believe you have a model

  p(y,theta) = p(theta|y) p(theta),

along with real data y and fake data y' and what
you'd like to do is calculate a sequential posterior

  p(theta|y') propto p(y'|theta) p(theta|y)

where p(theta|y) is the posterior for the model with data y.

Because

  p(theta|y) propto p(y|theta) p(theta)

this reduces to

  p(theta|y, y') propto p(y|theta) p(y'|theta) p(theta)

You can just write the joint model for that.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
You probably want to use a beta-binomial rather than
explicitly modeling theta[i].  And why cut a and b off at 1?

If you want to generate fake data based on the ongoing fit,
all you need to do is have:

data {
  int N_sim;
  int total[N_sim];
  ...

generated quantities {
  int success_sim[N_sim];
  for (int n in 1:N_sim)
    success_sim[n] <- beta_binomial_rng(total[n], a, b);
}

You could alternately take the totals and N_sim to be
the same as in the observed data.

If there's some other quantity you want, could you try to
write it out mathematically?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
We actually "fixed" the issue.  Now fabs(x) and abs(x)
are synonymous if x is real.  If n is an int, then
fabs(n) returns a real, whereas abs(n) returns an int.

We discussed this ages ago and decided it'd be less
confusing to have:

  real fabs(real);

  int abs(int);

as the only signatures, so we deprecated this one:

  real abs(real)

Do you (Andrew) think we should get rid of the deprecation
warning?

We could probably do away with fabs() altogether --- I think
it'd be sufficient for us to just have:

  int abs(int);

  real abs(real);

There would be no function that returned a real absolute value
for an int input, but I don't think we need that --- Stan already
lets you use an int in place of a real.

- Bob

This'd all be much easier to read if it was indented.

I'm still not sure what you mean by properties of a new
study needed to change your posterior.  Any new study will
change the posterior.  If it has exactly the same data
as the first study, the posterior intervals will become
narrower.

If you want to compare posteriors, just run one time with
the first set of data then a second time with the two sets of
data combined.

The point of sequential Bayesian inference is that it lets you
break apart observations into batches so you get the same answer
by updating a batch at a time, each time using the previous posterior
as a prior, as you would've gotten by just combining all the data
up front.

- Bob

Also, since today seems to be the day to promote
Krushcke's blog, check out his recommendations at:

http://doingbayesiandataanalysis.blogspot.com/2015/01/how-to-specify-informed-prior-in.html

Quick summary:  use a posterior sample to compute a
mean and covariance and then use the sample estimates as
parameters in a multi-normal prior.

- Bob

> On Jan 28, 2015, at 5:42 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> This'd all be much easier to read if it was indented.
>
> I'm still not sure what you mean by properties of a new
> study needed to change your posterior.  Any new study will
> change the posterior.  If it has exactly the same data
> as the first study, the posterior intervals will become
> narrower.
>
> If you want to compare posteriors, just run one time with
> the first set of data then a second time with the two sets of
> data combined.
>
> The point of sequential Bayesian inference is that it lets you
> break apart observations into batches so you get the same answer
> by updating a batch at a time, each time using the previous posterior
> as a prior, as you would've gotten by just combining all the data
> up front.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: Help with hierarchical linear model
messages.subject_clean: Help with hierarchical linear model
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am trying to develop a model with four nominal variables (age, gender, analysis method, disease type), and the interaction between some of these. The setup is a kind of repeated measures. Some of the participants have been measured 100+ times, other have been measured once. The response value is numerical. On a small dataset the model seems to perform as I would have expected, however on the full data set, with ~400k observations, the model is simply to slow. After 12 hours the model has not even gone through 500 iterations in any of the four chains run in parallel, whereas in the JAGS the roughly equivalent model took just under a day with ~10,000 iterations. I have tried to follow the guidelines for code optimisation in the manual plus what I have found in this forum.

What I would like to model is,

  y = a0 + a_S + a_age + a_sex + a_sex*age + a_analysis + a_type + a_age*type + a_sex*type + a_age*sex*type

a_S is the coefficient for each subject, modelled in as suggested by Kruschke (2010) for repeated measure experiments. I have precomputed all of the interactions in R, since I could not find a clever way of assigning each coefficient in Stan its own prior without a nested loop.

I have added a gist to the model file, and any comments on the model would be most welcome, both in terms of optimization but also scientific interpretation.

https://gist.github.com/demodw/4fe7e274bcbb76c0353a

Thanks!

David

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Help with hierarchical linear model
messages.body_plain:
We're all "real Stan folks"!

If you declare y as a vector, then you can define
the standardized version in one line as

  vector[Ntotal] zy;
  zy <- (y - mean(y)) / sd(y);

We should really implement a z_score() or standardize()
function to do this in one function call.

We go over which priors we recommend for regressions
in the manual regression chapter.  Short story is we
prefer softer constraints to hard intervals like you have.
(Warning: We haven't even updated all of our own examples to
follow our own advice yet!)

Is there a reason you're not giving the hierarchical
priors intercepts.  (Then the Matt trick, aka non-centered
parameterization, requires adding the mean back in.)

Without actually going into details of all the indices
on the predictors and effects, the basic structure looks
OK.

- Bob

> On Jan 30, 2015, at 11:37 AM, Jonah <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The real Stan folks can give you a more complete answer, but I noticed a few things that you can change that might help things out:
>
> 1. You can get rid of all the uniform(0,10) sampling statements and just declare the parameters with lower=0 and upper=10 constraints. Not sure how much this will help performance, but it certainly won't hurt.
>
> 2. You can use the "Matt trick" for all the normal priors on the coefficients. For example, for a0, you would do
>
> parameters {
>   a0_raw ;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>  a0 ;
>  a0 <- a0_raw * a0_sigma ;
> }
> model {
>  a0_raw ~ normal(0,1) ;
> }
>
> Making the sampling statements all for standard normals often helps quite a bit.
>
>

Some of the participants have been measured 100+ times, other have been measured once. The response value is numerical. messages.body_plain:
On Jan 30, 2015, at 1:59 PM, David Westergaard <da...@harsk.dk> wrote:
>
> I managed to implement the "Matt trick", though I had to convert my data type from real to vectors. I am not really sure what impact this has on performance, but hopefully it is better than ~18 hours for 500 iterations.

It's not the time per iteration that matters, but the time
per effective sample.  The non-centered parameterization will
mainly give you more effective samples per iteration, though
it can also speed up the iterations by requiring fewer leapfrog
steps.

You may not even need 500 iterations depending on how well
the model mixes with your data.

> Could you point me to the place on the reference manual where you discuss priors in regression?

There are several sections in the regression chapter.

Tightening priors (even if it doesn't have a noticeable impact
on the posterior) can be a big help with computation.  HMC
really likes to stretch its legs and explore when you give
it room to run.

> With regard to no intercept on the hierarchical priors, are you referring to the mean value of 0 on all coefficients? I actually started out by having hyperpriors on the coefficient mean, but I removed them since I was doing some debugging. Then plan is definitely to add them back, though.

Yes, that's what I meant.

- Bob

P.S.  Rob's working on implementing marginal maximum likelihood, so we
      should have a more general version of bglme soon.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dealing with (quasi)-complete separation with hierarchical logistic regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Dealing with (quasi)-complete separation with hierarchical logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
Xiao:
See my 2006 paper.  In short, never never inv_gamma(0.001,0.001).  Better to just do uniform.  Better still to use some weak prior info on the tau’s.  Also, parameterize the sd’s, not the variances.  Finally, for the regression coefficients, use soemthing stronger than normal(1,1000).  You could do N(0,10), which probably is still too broad but would probably be a better default start.
A

> On Jan 30, 2015, at 8:27 AM, Xiao He <xiao...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Dear all,
>
> Quasi-complete separation often occurs in data sets that I work with. I typically deal with it by using the blme package. For example, for this dataset at the end of this post, I use the model below:
>
> summary(bglmer(y ~ cond1 + (1|item) + (1|subject), data = data, family="binomial",  fixef.prior = normal(cov = diag(9,2))))
>
> And it works pretty well.  I wonder how I can do something similar in Stan. My current Stan model is below. However, the output is pretty bad (e.g., small effective n, large SEs of beta)). I wonder how I can impose a weakly informative prior in order to resolve the separation problem. Thanks!
>
>
> model.stan <- 'data {
> int<lower=1> N;
> int<lower=1> NS;
> int<lower=1> NI;
> int<lower=1, upper=NS> subject[N];
> int<lower=1, upper=NI> item[N];
> vector[N] cond1;
> int y[N];
> }
>
> parameters {
> vector[2] beta;
> real u[NS];
> real w[NI];
> real<lower=0> tau_u;
> real<lower=0> tau_w;
> }
> model{
> beta ~ normal(1, 1000);
> tau_u ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
> tau_w ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
> u ~ normal(0, sqrt(tau_u));
> w ~ normal(0, sqrt(tau_w));
>
> for(i in 1:N){
>    y[i] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(beta[1] + u[subject[i]] + w[item[i]] + beta[2]*cond1[i]));
> }
> }
> '
>
>
> stan.fit <-stan(model_code = model.stan, data = dat, iter = 1000, chains = 4)
>
>
> data <- structure(list(N = 265L, NS = 5L, NI = 59L, subject = c(1L, 1L,
> 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L,

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Help with hierarchical linear model
messages.body_plain:
Matt trick yes.  But I say no on the <lower=0,upper=10> thing.  I much prefer soft constraints.

> On Jan 30, 2015, at 11:37 AM, Jonah <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> The real Stan folks can give you a more complete answer, but I noticed a few things that you can change that might help things out:
>
> 1. You can get rid of all the uniform(0,10) sampling statements and just declare the parameters with lower=0 and upper=10 constraints. Not sure how much this will help performance, but it certainly won't hurt.
>
> 2. You can use the "Matt trick" for all the normal priors on the coefficients. For example, for a0, you would do
>
> parameters {
>   a0_raw ;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>  a0 ;
>  a0 <- a0_raw * a0_sigma ;
> }
> model {
>  a0_raw ~ normal(0,1) ;
> }
>
> Making the sampling statements all for standard normals often helps quite a bit.
>
>

>
> On Friday, January 30, 2015 at 5:45:14 AM UTC-5, David Westergaard wrote:

> > Hi everyone,
> >
> > I am trying to develop a model with four nominal variables (age, gender, analysis method, disease type), and the interaction between some of these. The setup is a kind of repeated measures. Some of the participants have been measured 100+ times, other have been measured once. The response value is numerical. On a small dataset the model seems to perform as I would have expected, however on the full data set, with ~400k observations, the model is simply to slow. After 12 hours the model has not even gone through 500 iterations in any of the four chains run in parallel, whereas in the JAGS the roughly equivalent model took just under a day with ~10,000 iterations. I have tried to follow the guidelines for code optimisation in the manual plus what I have found in this forum.
> >
> > What I would like to model is,
> >
> >   y = a0 + a_S + a_age + a_sex + a_sex*age + a_analysis + a_type + a_age*type + a_sex*type + a_age*sex*type
> >
> > a_S is the coefficient for each subject, modelled in as suggested by Kruschke (2010) for repeated measure experiments. I have precomputed all of the interactions in R, since I could not find a clever way of assigning each coefficient in Stan its own prior without a nested loop.
> >
> > I have added a gist to the model file, and any comments on the model would be most welcome, both in terms of optimization but also scientific interpretation.
> >
> > https://gist.github.com/demodw/4fe7e274bcbb76c0353a
> >
> > Thanks!
> >
> > David

messages.body_plain:
Andrew's current thinking on priors is summarized in three
sections (coeffs, scales, multivariate) of the regression chapter
of the Stan manual.

- Bob

> On Jan 30, 2015, at 4:06 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Xiao:
> See my 2006 paper.  In short, never never inv_gamma(0.001,0.001).  Better to just do uniform.  Better still to use some weak prior info on the tau’s.  Also, parameterize the sd’s, not the variances.  Finally, for the regression coefficients, use soemthing stronger than normal(1,1000).  You could do N(0,10), which probably is still too broad but would probably be a better default start.
> A
>
>
>> On Jan 30, 2015, at 8:27 AM, Xiao He <xiao...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Dear all,
>>
>> Quasi-complete separation often occurs in data sets that I work with. I typically deal with it by using the blme package. For example, for this dataset at the end of this post, I use the model below:
>>
>> summary(bglmer(y ~ cond1 + (1|item) + (1|subject), data = data, family="binomial",  fixef.prior = normal(cov = diag(9,2))))
>>
>> And it works pretty well.  I wonder how I can do something similar in Stan. My current Stan model is below. However, the output is pretty bad (e.g., small effective n, large SEs of beta)). I wonder how I can impose a weakly informative prior in order to resolve the separation problem. Thanks!
>>
>>
>> model.stan <- 'data {
>> int<lower=1> N;
>> int<lower=1> NS;
>> int<lower=1> NI;
>> int<lower=1, upper=NS> subject[N];
>> int<lower=1, upper=NI> item[N];
>> vector[N] cond1;
>> int y[N];

>> real u[NS];
>> real w[NI];

>> real<lower=0> tau_w;

>> beta ~ normal(1, 1000);
>> tau_u ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);

>> u ~ normal(0, sqrt(tau_u));
>> w ~ normal(0, sqrt(tau_w));
>>
>> for(i in 1:N){
>>    y[i] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(beta[1] + u[subject[i]] + w[item[i]] + beta[2]*cond1[i]));

2015-01-30 19:59 GMT+01:00 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:

> Thanks for sharing.
>
> There's a serious problem with the model as written.
> The parameter declaration:
>
> > parameters {
> >   real xi;
>
>
> is not consistent with the model:
>
> >   xi ~ uniform(-.5,.5);
>
> The general rule is that any parameter value matching the constraints
> (which here includes xi = 10, for example), should have support in
> the model.
>
> To fix, you need to declare:
>
>   real<lower=-0.5,upper=0.5> xi;
>
> If you don't, what will happen is that any path leading outside
> of (-0.5,0.5) will cause an immediate rejection and sampling can
> devolve.  You'll also get failed random initializations.
>
> We also don't recommend those very diffuse priors that were
> in the early BUGS models (or the interval constraints they switched
> to later).  There are a few sections in the regression chapter of
> the manual that we've added recently on what we do recommend.  It can
> also be a huge help with computation to have less diffuse priors, even
> if they're not informative enough to have a noticeable impact on the posterior.
>
> Maybe we should add the GEV density as a built-in.
>
> It's possible to speed up the implementation below with
> some algebra by treating y as a vector in the function.
> We'd eke out even more speed with a built-in version and also
> potentially avoid some calculations you don't need.
>
> The implementation below would be faster if you converted
> everything to vectors, but it's not so straightorward to write
> because we don't have a vector version of pow(), so I had
> to define some intermediates to avoid redundant calculations.
> I haven't tried to validate this does the right thing, but
> it'd look something like this:
>
> real gev_log (vector y, real mu, real sigma, real xi) {
>   vector[size(y)] z;
>   vector[size(y) + 1] lp;
>   real inv_xi;
>   real inv_xi_p1;
>   real neg_inv_xi;
>   z <- ((1 + y) - mu) * (xi / sigma);
>   inv_xi <- inv(xi);
>   inv_xi_p1 <- 1 + inv_xi;
>   neg_inv_xi <- -inv_xi;
>   for (n in 1:size(y))
>     lp[n] <-  inv_xi_p1 * log(z[n]) + pow(z[n],neg_inv_xi);
>   lp[size(y) + 1] <- size(y) * log(sigma);
>   return -sum(lp);
> }
>
> and then it's just
>
>   y ~ gev(mu,sigma,xi);
>
> in the model.  This should be quite a bit faster than the
> simpler implementation.  But then it may not be worth the ugliness
> if it's already fast enough.
>
> I may pull this out as an optimization case study for the manual.
>
> - Bob
>
> >     real z;
> >     z <- 1 + (y - mu) * xi / sigma;
> >
> >   }
>
>
> data {p
>   vector[N] y;
>
> - Bob
>

> >
> > functions {

> >     z <- 1 + (y - mu) * xi / sigma;
> >     return -log(sigma) - (1 + 1/xi)*log(z) - pow(z,-1/xi);

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan. I'm very interested in this; maybe I can collect together the various requests and come to a future Stan dev meeting to help figure out priorities. (Not this coming week, but later is fine.)

A related question that I expect there'd be much interest in is sparse matrix operations. Is there an issue page for that on the repository / have there already been discussions?

To answer the meta-question: I think with functions Stan can already handle the calculation of a Kronecker matrix-vector product (K1 \otimes K2)v but not (K1 \otimes K2 \otimes K3) v.

Seth
